speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. FLEMING (EGLINTON)  REFERENCE TO RE- MARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 9
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Last evening when I was not in the house the hon. member for Assiniboia made certain statements which I think reflect on me. They are to be found on pages 2841 and 2844 of Hansard, and I read them:
A few weeks ago the Minister of Finance said in this house that one of the reasons why there is so much trouble today with regard to unemployment is because of the wartime babies. He said there were too many wartime babies and they are now old enough to be on the labour market. He said, "We cannot deal with the love life of Canadians and the new citizens we have who are coming of working age. There were too many wartime babies." We asked why so many people are on the unemployment rolls. "Too many pregnant women drawing unemployment insurance who should not be receiving it." Some answer.
That is on page 2841. On page 2844 the hon. member said further:
The Minister of Finance said that one of the reasons the government was having a difficult time achieving a full employment economy was the high birth rate during the war. If the hon. gentleman will read the remarks carefully he will find this in the speech.
And further, speaking of myself the hon. member said:
He said that this was the reason unemployment was so high and he could not do anything about it.
And again:
Except there were too many people coming of employment age and the government could not do anything about employment.
The remarks attributed to me, Mr. Speaker, have never been uttered by me. What I did say on this subject is a matter of record in the house and could have been quoted precisely from the record by any hon. member wishing to refer to my remarks in their proper context. They are to be found on page 1001 of Hansard and read as follows:
.. . the growth of our labour force is now more directly attributable to the coming of age, from an employment point of view at least, of the large number of babies who were born in Canada during and immediately after the war.
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the remarks attributed to me by the hon. member
for Assiniboia bear no resemblance whatever to what I actually did say, and the best that can be said for his remarks is that they are an irresponsible distortion of what I said.

I wonder whether the minister has given sufficient reason for deferring his objection. After all, he was in the house last night when the remarks about which he now wishes to complain were made, and I am very sceptical about the desirability of a practice which allows members to go back and pick up what has been said and debate the matter. subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF AMBASSADOR TO CERTAIN CENTRAL AMERICAN REPUBLICS
speechtext:
On January 20 I informed the house that the Canadian government and the governments of the republics of Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama had decided to establish diplomatic

Appointment of Ambassador relations. I now wish to announce the appointment of Mr. Jean-Louis Delisle as ambassador of Canada to these four Central American republics. Mr. Delisle will normally reside in Costa Rica but will pay regular visits to the other three countries to which he is accredited. The Canadian embassy in Costa Rica will be opened next week under a charge d'affaires ad interim, pending Mr. Delisle's arrival in May. Arrangements are being made for reciprocal representation of the four republics in Ottawa.
Mr. Delisle, a native of Quebec city, is a career foreign service officer who has served Canada with distinction at home and abroad for nearly 20 years. He is a graduate in law from Laval University and holds a degree from Oxford, where he was a Rhodes scholar in 1939. Since joining the Department of External Affairs in 1942 he has served in Rio de Janeiro, Boston, and Warsaw, where he was charge d'affaires from 1954 until 1957. In the following year he served as a member of the United Nations commission in Togoland which paved the way for that country's independence in 1960. Subsequently he served as head of the legal division of the Department of External Affairs and since September 1959 has been counsellor in charge of press and cultural relations at the Canadian embassy in Paris.
Central America has been until now one of the areas in which Canada was seriously under-represented, mainly because of the heavy demands that have been made on a growing foreign service in other parts of the world. The government's decision to expand Canada's relations with that area is a further step in a policy of fostering closer economic, political and cultural ties with Latin America as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have leave of the house to draw to its attention that today, March 10, 1961, is a day of great significance to Canadians of Ukrainian origin, being the centennial of the death of their greatest hero and poet, Taras Shevchenko. His name is worshipped by 45 million Ukrainians wherever they may be found, and by some half million of that race in Canada who have integrated themselves in the Canadian way of life and who can be counted as constituents of most of the members of this house.
Taras Shevchenko, the son of a Ukrainian serf, who was a free man for only nine years of his short life, died when he was 47. His pen proved to be more powerful than the decrees of the oppressors of his people, and by his unfaltering faith in the victory of democratic ideals, despite all obstacles he became the greatest poet and freedom fighter of the Slavonic world. He is not only a national figure among a given people but a luminous personality in the world course of contemporary history. His poetic works-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES TARAS SHEVCHENKO    ANNIVERSARY OF DEATH OF UKRAINIAN POET
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has asked for the leave of the house and by its indulgence has called attention to this very interesting anniversary, but if he is to take more time he must have the expressed leave of the house to continue?

maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES TARAS SHEVCHENKO    ANNIVERSARY OF DEATH OF UKRAINIAN POET
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES TARAS SHEVCHENKO    ANNIVERSARY OF DEATH OF UKRAINIAN POET
speechtext:
His poetic works deal not only with the oppression of his own people but also with the enslavement of every other nation raped by the white despot of his time and by the red imperialist of today. To his own people his works "Kobzar" are the national gospel and are to be found in nearly every home. His fiery words resurrected a nation thought to be dead; they inspired his people to deeds of heroism in their struggle for independence and give them hope and courage in bondage. He calls to all to "rise

and break the chains" and, echoing a passage from la Marseillaise, to "spatter freedom with evil enemy blood". He calls for brotherly love among the Slav family of nations.
His works are not only popular among his own people. They have been translated into all Slavonic languages as well as into English, French, German, Italian and Swedish. To his immortal name those of his origin in Canada are erecting a monument in the grounds of the Manitoba legislature in Winnipeg because, as a poet, he not only enriched the literature of his own people but inspired them with new hope for freedom. What he sought for them he sought for the oppressed everywhere in the world. This monument is to be unveiled on July 15 of this year, and gratitude goes to the government of Manitoba for permitting its erection.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you and, through you, the members of this house for having given me the opportunity to make this statement.

maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES TARAS SHEVCHENKO    ANNIVERSARY OF DEATH OF UKRAINIAN POET
speechtext:
The house has unanimously agreed to lay aside its procedures in order to permit the hon. gentleman to pay tribute to one of the great poets of the Ukraine, Taras Shevchenko. It is appropriate that hon. members should join with the hon. member for Marquette in marking the anniversary of this great Ukrainian who in his poetry has given justification for the hopes of contemporary Ukrainians for the liberation of their homeland.
In doing so we can recognize that there are many Shevchenkos in every ethnic group in our country, who likewise give cause for hope of liberation from totalitarian oppression which has now taken hold of so many of them. The hon. member is a Canadian of Ukrainian descent. He may be assured that those of us in the Liberal party recognize the great contribution made by the Ukrainian people to the building up of this nation, as indeed we recognize the contribution made by so many other ethnic groups toward building up this country, the most envied country among the nations of the world, despite its current difficulties.

Mr. Speaker, the report in the Winnipeg Free Press is quite incorrect. Therefore the question which the hon. member has based on it contains statements and assumptions that are also incorrect.
This is the actual basis of the matter. On the University of Manitoba campus there is apparently a ban the bomb organization and also an organization called the students' association for nuclear armament. Apparently some members of the latter organization, who are members of the cadet training corps, posted a notice on Department of National Defence property that a meeting of the association would be held there. As a result the co-ordinator for university military training wrote a letter to army cadets only indicating 90205-6-181
Inquiries of the Ministry that regular force personnel-R.O.T.P. subsidized officer cadets and second lieutenants- are not permitted to become members of
S.	A.N.A., the student association for nuclear armament or to participate in S.A.N.A. activities. The letter went on to say that reserve personnel-U.N.T.D., C.O.T.C., U.R.-
T.	P.-who choose to belong to S.A.N.A. as private citizens must not participate in the activities of S.A.N.A. in their capacity as members of the armed forces and, finally, that the armed forces office is not to be used for meetings of the students' association for nuclear armament.
I think nothing was sent out to the students in connection with any other organization, and the only reason the letter was sent was that a notice had been posted on Department of National Defence property of a meeting to be held on departmental property. This action was taken in view of queen's regulations and orders, section 19-36 of which lays down among other things that no officer or man shall, without permission, publish his opinions on any military question that is under consideration by superior authorities. There were no specific instructions issued apart from these, so far as I know.
The whole story is really entirely incorrect. I understand that the reporter who wrote the story telephoned the R.C.A.F. staff officer, who was not in at the time, represented himself to the corporal on duty as an R.C.A.F. officer, and sought to get information in connection with this matter. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, we all agree that the act of 1918, though very well drafted, had become obsolete and needed some changes. We had hoped for that. Besides, it was the St. Laurent administration that had asked the civil service commission to inquire and determine what could be done to improve the situation. The minister is introducing today a bill that bears very close resemblance to the one introduced last year and in that regard we might say that if the former legislation had a white beard, this new bill is almost antediluvian, because instead of moving forward, it is moving backwards.
We note a bad and dangerous tendency in the new act because it might vest with increased powers the governor in council and thus the ministers and department heads, the deputy heads and their subordinates, without any provision enabling the civil service commission to interfere in order to prevent any abuses in that regard.
The Civil Service Association of Canada complained about this last year and I am convinced it will continue to do so, because this is what I read on page 5 of the C.S.A.C. journal for January 1961:
(Text):
This reference is to Bill No. C-77, not the bill we are studying today:
Under the present Civil Service Act, (i.e. chapter 48 R.S.C. 1952) the civil service commission has the statutory power and obligation to report upon any matter pertaining to the organization or proposed organization of the various departments. As a protection to the merit principle, this would seem to be a wise provision, and experience over the years would indicate that every possible safeguard to this principle must be maintained in the law.
The proposal in Bill C-77 takes from the civil service commission the authority or right to make such reports except at the request of the deputy head. We are opposed to this provision and urge that the right to make such reports still be vested in the civil service commission.
(Translation):
In fact, Mr. Speaker, that remark by the Civil Service Association of Canada is quite relevant; because, if wider powers were 90205-6-181i
Civil Service Act
granted to the governor in council or to ministers, as well as to chiefs of departments, that is to say to deputy ministers or their subordinates, and if those powers were used in such a way as not to always satisfy the employees, the morale of the employees might suffer, and if the morale of the employees is not good, their work will be the less efficient.
The increase in the number of prevailing rates employees is another matter of concern and trouble in this bill. Civil servants regret that the government seems to wish to obtain that right, even if it does not intend to exercise it-I do not wish to impute motives either to the Minister of Finance or to the Secretary of State-but when powers are granted to them, there is always the danger that those powers be taken literally and that they may be used to increase the number of prevailing rates employees. I agree that under certain circumstances, it may be necessary, and I refer, for instance, to the census which comes once every ten years and which obviously requires a considerable number of supplementary employees, some for three months, others for six months, and a few others even for a year. Therefore, it is normal that those employees be considered as prevailing rates employees, but there shoqld be no provision in the act to allow ministers, the governor in council, deputy ministers, or their subordinates, to suggest a too substantial increase in the number of those employees, because those who start in a department intend to make a career there that is, to prepare their future and ensure their living for their old age.
What will happen to the security of employment in the civil service if it can be decided over night that the prevailing rates shall apply? This makes the situation intolerable for federal employees. It will surely be reflected in their work, and the qualified employees will seek employment in private industry rather than in the public service.
Besides, if we consider the report commonly known as the Heeney report, which is the report of the civil service commission, tabled in December 1958, we find concerning the morale of the employees, the following statement on page 10:
Maintain good morale by clarifying the rights and obligations of employees.
It seems that the government scorned the wish expressed by the Heeney commission to see to it that public servants enjoy a greater measure of security in order to give better service.
The merit system is essential if we want our employees to enjoy the sound morale which will mean a better service. To this end, it is important to clearly define and allot the

Civil Service Act
authority conferred upon each party. The cabinet should not be given the right to interfere too often in this field or to ignore the decisions of the civil service commission.
The commission should be and remain a lot more independent of the executive, because its members are not interested in politics. They are more interested in the smooth working of the civil service, because of their past experience.
We know that when the Civil Service Act was enacted in 1918 the commission hardly numbered 40,000 employees, with the majority of them working as clerks at different levels. However, in the meantime, the responsibilities of the civil service commission have increased. At the time we were merely a British colony, and, consequently had less responsibilities than we have now. With the passing of the Statute of Westminster in 1927, which was finally signed in 1931, Canada became an autonomous country and government departments grew larger and more numerous. This, in turn, increased the responsibilities of civil servants and, at the same time those of the civil service commission.
During the war, the number of civil servants grew to an almost terrific extent. Many of them accepted positions of permanent character because the country's new status was compelling the government to multiply its services.
The post-war period brought about the recognition of Canada as an international power and an unprecedented development took place in the Department of External Affairs thus requiring new categories of employees.
There was growth too in the research branch. A considerable number of scientists offered their services to the state to the advantage of all Canadians.
The number of federal civil servants grew so much that the civil service commission had to take special precautions in order to retain its employees of unusual merit.
Now that cannot be achieved unless the civil service commission remains free to establish its own regulations and to develop its services without undue government interference and, above all, provided it has the upper hand on the often arbitrary decisions, as they were described by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), of division heads and deputy ministers. Well, the line should be more clearly, more accurately drawn.

Mr. Speaker, since I do not have Hansard here. I accept the correction made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, and I say that a few minor officials use their authority to impose their views, sometimes unduly. Therefore it is necessary that the civil service commission have greater, instead of reduced powers. Besides, I see in paragraph 10, page 9 of the Heeney report, the following remarks:
Clearer definition of the division of authority and responsibility for decision as between departments of government on the one hand and, on the other, the commission, to which, as a body independent of the executive, certain functions are assigned by parliament;
And further on:
-subject only to such safeguards as may be necessary to maintain the merit principle-
And again:
-a program that will, within a reasonable time, result in "One Civil Service" in which all are subject to the same standards of obligation and benefit;
And further,
Greater participation by employees in the processes leading to the determination of their conditions of employment.
Those are conclusions of the Heeney report requesting the government to grant that recommendation and I am now requesting the same thing today. The sound administration of the civil service calls for a clear definition of those points and it is particularly necessary that the civil service commission retain its powers.
The commission should remain independent so that no minister or deputy minister may, alone, through a decision of his own, bring about changes without a recommendation to the civil service commission. Final decisions should never be left to ministers nor to deputy ministers or their subordinates.
There should be set up a board or court duly empowered to deal with the appeals of those civil servants who feel that they have been unfairly treated.
Admittedly such appeals are being heard at the present time but the Heeney commission did in fact recommend a widening of the grounds for appeal and an improved and more judicial procedure in this respect.
I think that at the moment, while grievances of deputy ministers and their subordinates are heard, proceedings are practically in camera, which means that those people are sent away and then the appellant or plaintiff

is called without having heard what the other had said. They are thus being placed in a position of inferiority. Moreover, they are entitled to call on an employee or a member of an association to defend them, but they have not been allowed to call upon a lawyer to help them prepare their case.
I think there should exist in the civil service commission as in the unemployment insurance commission a tribunal before which any employee could bring his case and even be defended by a lawyer. Complaints would be made while the appealing party and the person involved in the complaint are present. In his examination the lawyer could, possibly through appropriate questions, bring out contradictions and ascertain whether the complaint is well-founded or if it is only because of some personal spite or grudge that the employee is in a difficult situation.
Both sides should be given a chance to explain why suspension or dismissal is recommended. Employees would then feel more secure especially as regards promotions.
Civil servants often complain-I do not say that they are right-that they were denied deserved promotions. Well, how can you prove whether they are right or wrong if there is no tribunal to hear complaints and find out if there was a well-founded reason for denying a promotion?
I know of a case of a person whom I know very well. He is a French Canadian who tried and passed every examination for a certain position. As he always came out first the head of the department applied to have the position abolished so that he would not get the promotion. If there had been an appeal tribunal, that man could have had his case heard before the abolition of that particular position, he could have found out why a competition had been opened and then, following the examination, why application had been made to have the position abolished.
This is one case in a thousand, because since I have been a member of this house I have received a voluminous correspondence telling me of the complaints of dissatisfied people. I do not pretend that this has happened only under this government

it existed before, but it is, however, a lack that should be filled now by an amendment to this new bill. That is why I suggest that the government disregarded the justified complaints of the small employees who are just as much entitled to be defended as the higher-ups.
Civil Service Act
Besides, if the appealing party could call on a lawyer, he would have much better protection, since it is not everybody who can state his complaint quite clearly; in fact, a civil servant may be a perfect clerk who perfectly knows his work, but when he has to appear before an appeal board where it is important to express himself well, not being used to public speaking, he cannot defend himself easily in a case of this kind, while if he had his own counsel, he could rely on him to relieve him of his sudden uneasiness and state his case much more clearly.
Besides, at page 16 of the civil service commission report, I read something about the appeals in paragraph 38:
With these considerations in mind, the commission's proposals are designed to place firmly on the departments primary responsibility to maintain discipline while, at the same time, providing suitable safeguards against uneven or unfair treatment of employees.
Therefore, the civil service commission
itself had realized there had been unjust treatment of certain cases, and that there had been no means to cure this situation because of the excessive power of certain divisional heads.
Our proposals entail among other things,
(c)	that the scope of appeals to the commission in such matters be substantially broadened;
(d)	that dismissal be effected by the commission on the recommendation of the deputy head (instead of by an order in council); and
(e)	that, before an employee is dismissed on grounds of political partisanship, his case be fully investigated and reported upon by one or more commissioners appointed for the purpose under part I of the Enquiries Act.
As you see, Mr. Speaker, what I am saying has been provided for in the civil service commission report. So, it is not new, and I suggest that we should act upon this.
And here is another weakness existing within the civil service, and it is the famous rating. As far as this question of rating is concerned, the same standard should be applied by all departments without exception. When this rating of the employee is ready for submission to the civil service commission- the rating factor is important for promotion- it should be submitted to the civil servant for his acceptance or refusal. If he feels that his chief who has given him this rating was unfair, he should have the right to appeal to the civil service commission and that right of appeal should be recognized in the act, but it is not so now.
There is only one department that I know of-there may be others of which I am not

Civil Service Act
aware-but we have the Department of National Defence where employees, accustomed to those efficiency reports in the army where a soldier, when shown his report, could appeal to his superior officer, maintained the same procedure. Since that practice existed in the army, it has been applied to the civilian staff of that department. They are asked to sign the report and if any objection is raised, then the report is discussed and often amended.
I can say that when I was myself an employee of the civil service in 1927, I have seen cases where there was an injustice because a head of department did not like a subaltern's mug. I suppose that the same situation still exists.
We live with men who unfortunately labour under certain human frailties and tend towards feelings of unreasond likes or dislikes. That is why, when the time comes to discuss this particular point, this should be corrected by standardizing the rating. In addition, the civil service commission should have the right to legislate in that field, to hear the appeal of the employee who feels he has been discriminated against, the appeal being heard in the presence of both the author of the efficiency report and the appellant to prevent any discussion behind closed doors. Thus one day, great and small will be able to be treated fairly in the civil service.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is the question of salaries. It has been brought up often during these last few years especially by civil servants who, I feel, were quite right in their complaints.
In the January issue of their newspaper, here is what I find on page 7:
(Text):
Canadian civil servants have a right to play a definite role in determining their wages, salaries and working conditions. Clause 7-
That is clause 7 of the bill.
-does not provide even an elementary basis for a proper system of negotiation.
We would therefore urge, with all the emphasis we can muster, that this committee amend clause 7 to read as follows:
"The cabinet, or such ministers or minister, or officer or officers of the crown it may designate, is empowered to negotiate directly and consult with representatives of appropriate associations and organizations of employees of the crown on all matters of personnel administration in the public service, including remuneration and all other terms and conditions of employment under regulations and procedures drawn under the provisions of this act. Such direct negotiation and consultation shall be initiated by the cabinet or its appointees

on the one hand, and by recognized staff associations and organizations on the other hand.
"The provisions of such regulations as may be drawn should also include provision for arbitration of issues which cannot be settled by negotiation".
(Translation) :
I fully agree with the civil service association on this point.
Besides, I suggested last year, when Bill C-77 was introduced-it was later withdrawn -that whenever negotiations dealt with salaries or working conditions, civil service organizations should be called in and should have a representative sitting with the commission, in order that their views might be known. In this way, what happened in the past would not happen again, such as the issuing of a secret and confidential report which nobody knew anything about and to which nobody could refer before its publication. That famous report caused serious injustice. If I am not mistaken, salary increases started to be granted in April. One group of employees got their increase as of the 1st of April, another group on the 1st of May, another on the 1st of June and so on each month until September.
Raises were therefore granted class by class. They were retroactive only to the first of the month in which the recommendation was made to the house by the minister.
This means that employees of equal merit did not get their increase until September, and were refused those rights enjoyed by those who had had their raise in April, May or June.
That Mr. Speaker, was a glaring injustice which moved the employees to bitter complaint and properly so. Had they taken part in the discussions, had they been entitled to attend the negotiations, they would have known what was going on and they would have shared the secrets of the powers that be.
They could have then made representations to the commission, to the department and also put their case before the people of Canada through the newspapers, if they were being treated unfairly.
Moreover I find that my request is not in contradiction with the terms of the Heeney report. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to page 132, appendix (b). The Heeney report is totally in agreement with this request since it says:
For 14 years, organized civil servants have possessed in the national joint council-
And further on:
The opinion is widely held that the council could play a more active role in this area with

advantage to both employer and employees. We share this view and consider that the time has come for a re-examination of the terms of reference and procedures of the council, with the object of strengthening its position and prestige, and making it a more useful and effective body for joint consultation.
That recommendation of the civil service commission has been completely ignored, completely disregarded.
Yet, the minister told us that section 7 provided for meetings between employees, at their request, with the department or the commission. But those recommendations may be accepted or refused by the department. So, if it were enacted that employees are entitled to share in negotiations, the department could not turn them down; it could no longer say: "You cannot have this," or "You are not entitled to that", because it would have to accept it.
That is a recommendation made by the civil service commission after a thorough investigation of this matter. And in section 3 of appendix (b) we find this:
The last authorized view coming from the government was that of the Prime Minister, expressed on May 1, 1958,
That is the present Prime Minister, who is now in London. He expressed this view on May 1, 1958:
-in an address delivered before one of the large staff organizations:
Please note, Mr. Speaker, that I am quoting no less a person than the Prime Minister of Canada. Only a few years ago, he stated, and I quote:
I think that civil servants, through their associations' representatives, should have a greater say in the establishment of salary scales in the civil service. A more rational method should be adopted whereby your ideas and advice could influence the application of principles on which there is nearly full agreement in matters of salary.
The Prime Minister was in agreement. They were supposed to enjoy more consideration, but I do not know what happened to change that approach, because this is not included, as it was not included in Bill C-77, introduced at the last session.
Section 4 reads as follows:
On the side of the employees, the associations have, over a considerable period, advocated the introduction in one form or another of negotiating procedures and "collective bargaining". Some have pressed for the amendment of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act so as to include civil servants and open to organized government employees the processes of negotiation, conciliation and arbitration for which that statute provides. Some have advocated the establishment of a special arbitration tribunal whose awards, in the event of failure of agreement,
Civil Service Act
would be binding on both sides. No recognized association has asserted on behalf of civil servants the right to strike.
Therefore, it is clearly established that no recognized association has claimed the right to strike, and I think they were right in that. Now, the right to strike under special circumstances is a sacred and a natural right of self-defence against abuse by certain companies. But government employees have a higher duty toward their country than certain labour associations. So civil servants have no intention of claiming the right to strike, but they do claim the right of association and even the right to arbitration.
To my mind this would not deprive parliament of any of its privileges because, in the final analysis, parliament would set salaries when estimates of the civil service commission are before us, so that the last word in the matter would remain with parliament. Furthermore, claims made by associations of civil servants and joint decisions reached may not be considered by nor will be binding on parliament except for the voting of estimates.
Section 5 has to do with joint committees and here is how it reads:
Although officials of the principal staff associations are in regular and frequent contact-
Allow me to point out, Mr. Speaker, that this is an answer to the assertions of the minister, an answer to section 7 of the bill now under discussion.
... are in regular and frequent contact with the commission on questions of pay, there has so far been no systematic procedure for discussion of these matters between representatives of the employees and representatives of the government. In our opinion, this is an unsatisfactory situation from every point of view. Civil servants compare their position unfavourably in this respect with that of other employees; neither side has adequate opportunity to explain its case; the inevitable consequence is the resort to pressure tactics and public controversy.
That is the whole point. Civil servants must be granted the rights normally enjoyed by human beings to have their representations heard regularly without having to go hat in hand to the cabinet or the commission, but through rights clearly defined in the act, they must be enabled to say: "We are coming here on behalf of those we represent, on behalf of associations, to ask for such conditions and such a salary." The final decision will remain with parliament, but we must give civil servants the right to make representations.
And further on, I read:
Representation of the employees affected would be provided from the staff association which, for the purpose, would have to establish suitable joint machinery.

vivil Service Act
We should supply the suitable machinery, and this is not something I have dreamed up, it is stated in the civil service commission report. The government should, through amendments to the act, provide the suitable machinery; it should not be a time to time affair, but machinery perfectly and clearly defined which would give civil servants the right to be heard when necessary.
Again on the same subject, here is what we find in section 10 of appendix (b):
An Important element in any such regime would be that the commission's recommendations subsequent to the conduct of discussions should be communicated simultaneously to the government and to the staff associations concerned. Final decision on the commission's recommendations would, of course, remain a matter for the government, subject to the ultimate will of parliament.
And in section 12, we read the following:
We therefore recommend:
They are the recommendations of the civil service commission.
We therefore recommend:
That the government request the commission-
Listen carefully, for this is clear and explicit:
That the government request the commission- commission, in consultation with officials of the treasury board on the one hand, and the staff associations on the other, to develop and institute procedures along the lines described above for the participation of government employees in the determination of compensation in the civil service-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, constituting as it does the first revision and modernization of the Civil Service Act in 43 years is of very high significance and vital, long range consequence. Since it is proposed that it shall be referred to a special committee for detailed study, a committee in which I hope to take an active part, my contribution at this time will be less extended than it would otherwise be.
I do not propose to refer in detail to the speeches which have been made earlier in the debate. My failure to do so is not to be interpreted in any way as an indication, even by inference, that I agree with all that has been said in the debate thus far. Indeed, with one speech which was made I profoundly disagree. I do not deny, sir, that abuses occasionally do occur in personnel administration. Civil servants are as human as any

other citizens, but I do assert with the greatest of confidence that abuses are very much the exception rather than the rule. That is all I propose to say at this time in respect of that, sir. There will be an opportunity in the special committee where, if necessary, I will make my views known in greater detail.
The Civil Service Act of 1918 is a lasting monument to the government of Sir Robert Borden, and in its day it was the most advanced measure of public service reform in any country in the world. It firmly established the merit principle as an instrument of national policy; it banished the old spoils system, the nepotism and favouritism which had plagued us in earlier days. The mere fact that after 22 years of government by one party a change of government could take place, as it did in June of 1957, with the least upset to the civil service of any change of government in our history, is the best evidence of how firmly embedded the principles of the Civil Service Act of 1918 had become, and how firmly was the adherence of the Progressive Conservative party to those principles.
All but one of those who have spoken previously in this debate have emphasized how Canadians everywhere have reason to be proud of the standards and calibre of our civil service. I have said before in this house, and I repeat it now, that at international conferences and at learned societies as well as in the performance of day to day duties, our Canadian public servants can meet on at least equal terms the public servants of any other country.
In modernizing the Civil Service Act after 43 years I submit that parliament must be guided by two basic and associated objectives. The first must be to maintain and constantly improve the standards and quality of our public service. The second, and the companion objective, must be to make a civil service career at least as satisfying, as attractive and rewarding as any professional or business career. We must encourage a high proportion of our young people of exceptional talent to enter and remain in the public service. We must give to a civil service career the status and respect which will be an incentive, a stimulus to the young, highly educated men and women in the sciences, in the professions, in administration and in other basic fields to offer their services to the state.
Too often uninformed public opinion tends to look upon career civil servants as persons

looking for an easy spot where they can avoid the stress of competitive society as in business or in a profession. Such a public attitude is, in my opinion, totally unjustified and unfair. I believe that the overwhelming majority of our public servants are conscientious, hard working and effective.
What I have been trying to say was put very neatly by Mr. Neil McElroy, former United States secretary of defence and now chairman of the board of Procter and Gamble Limited, in a speech last November 22, when he said this:
We must recognize their contribution to our nation's progress and give them proper status in the public esteem.
Moreover, they must be adequately compensated. No one expects a government career to offer wealth. It has its other valued compensations. Like teaching or the ministry, it is a dedicated service. It can offer satisfactions in personal accomplishments and fulfilment for which, for many, there is no substitute. Government service, if it means to us what it should, must have its justified place in the consideration of careers by the young people of the country.
That expresses, I believe, the attitude which parliament must adopt in this important task of modernizing the Civil Service Act. As parliamentarians, as the elected representatives of the people, we must recognize that it is to the career civil service that we must look for long range continuity and experienced competence in our government. However able may be the ministry, however dedicated and sincere may be the front bench of any political party, they can succeed in their tasks only with the loyal support, the objective and disinterested advice and administrative competence of thousands upon thousands of career civil servants. And so, sir, I hope parliament and the special committee will submit this bill to certain basic tests and ascertain if it does, as I believe it does, meet certain standards.
The first standard or test is the preservation intact of the merit principle. Upon that cornerstone we must build. There must be an assurance that it is in fact, however, a genuine merit system. Parliament wants the genuine practice of the merit system, not a system of lip service to it. The mere abolition of the spoils system, the abandonment and prevention of political patronage or favouritism, is not in itself assurance that the merit system truly prevails. The Heeney report speaks of what it describes as "bureaucratic patronage" as being less apparent but no less insidious and demoralizing than political patronage. With that I fully agree.
In this new act and in its administration I hope that that may be avoided. I hope we 90205-6-182
Civil Service Act
will have the assurance that appointments and promotions are made on the basis of an objective determination of the relative merits of qualified candidates. We have that assurance, and I think we must have an assurance as well that there will be safeguards against any internal abuses, against any favouritism, against what the Heeney report described, as I have said, as "bureaucratic patronage".
The second standard or test to which I think we must submit this bill is whether it preserves fully the independent status of the civil service commission. That it does, in my opinion. Since 1918 the commission has enjoyed a quasi-judicial status. That position, in my opinion, is fundamental to the establishment of sound principles of recruitment and promotion.
The third test to which the house and the committee will wish to submit this bill, in my opinion, is whether it will provide increased flexibility of administration as well as greater simplicity of procedures. As I read the bill, sir, the division of authority between the commission and the deputy heads will be more clearly defined, that of the commission in recruitment and promotion being reinforced whereas in direct managerial matters, for speed and ease of decision, which are very important factors, a greater authority will be vested in deputy heads. The house must always remember, I think, that organization and classification play as significant roles in standards and conditions of work as do recruitment, promotion or pay.
One of the results which I hope will flow from this legislation is a more positive use of planned transfers as between departments. The Heeney report spoke of this as a means of providing promising civil servants with more productive and more attractive careers, and with that I most heartily agree. It will avoid good men getting into blind alleys or following well travelled ruts. I hope that a positive program of interdepartmental transfers will be pursued in order to broaden the experience and increase the knowledge of promising young career men and women.
The fourth standard by which the bill must be tested is that which has had perhaps the greatest publicity, the question of increasing participation of civil servants and their associations in all the processes leading to the determination of pay and other conditions of employment. The amendment made to the draft bill as presented last year enables the staff associations to initiate consultations and discussions, and of that I enthusiastically approve. The basic issue that is before the house

Civil Service Act
and will be before the committee is whether the techniques ought to be embodied in the detailed provisions of the law. Should the processes of consultation and the results to flow from consultation be spelled out in the statute?
As I see it, sir, parliament is embarking upon a totally new adventure in the field of employer-employee relations, and my own view is that the techniques, like freedom, ought to broaden down from precedent to precedent. My hon. friends from Ottawa East and Hull now profess a lifetime of undying devotion to the full application of the principle of collective bargaining to civil service employment. With respect, I suggest that their conversion has come somewhat late in life.
The hon. member for Hull sought to have the Liberal rally as late as January, 1961, endorse collective bargaining, and with what result? It was turned back by the subcommittee; it was referred to the policy committee for further study, and it has never yet seen the light of day. What that much vaunted Liberal rally refused to endorse my hon. friends place before the house as Liberal policy.

If the hon. member is now saying that the national joint council is a process of collective bargaining, I have never heard him assert it before in the house. I say to him that now that a major and constructive step has been taken, hon. gentlemen opposite seek to criticize it and to pretend that they have always believed in something more. I have always found actions more convincing than professions.
What this bill does is to provide a framework within which procedures and techniques of consultation may develop and expand to the mutual advantage of government and civil servant. This is not a strait-jacket; it is a guide to future progress in a field fraught with not a few problems, and staff associations and others are aware of these problems. In my opinion these new provisions will call for constructive statesmanship on the part of the leaders of staff associations as well as representatives of the government. Responsible, temperate, accountable stewardship will lead to constructive results in the application of clause 7. Good will and cordiality will achieve what immoderation of language and action would simply throw away.
The bill in my view is the culmination of a series of major and constructive advances in civil service administration achieved under the leadership of the present Prime Minister. I give but a few examples; the establishment of the pay research bureau, increases for superannuated civil servants, revision of the Public Service Superannuation Act to provide inter alia a six-year average, the institution of a modern medical-surgical plan, the appointment on every practical occasion of deputy ministers from within the ranks of the service, the institution of a system of class by class salary increases with periodic reviews based on the principle of fair comparison, the appointment of the Glassco commission to study the organization of government generally, and now this bill.
This is the record of achievement under the leadership of the present Prime Minister with the support of the Minister of Finance. I believe that more genuine progress in civil service administrative reform, in conditions of employment and pay, has been made in the past three years than in any comparable period in our history.
This, I believe, is a good bill. It may well be that the conscientious, non-partisan study of the special committee can make it a better bill. From that study and from the bill when ultimately enacted I hope there will emerge a civil service act which will bring pride

of status to every civil servant, and which will stand as a example to all legislatures in the world interested in the application of the merit system.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make at this stage of the bill. I think it is a well known fact that the only political party in Canada that has had any consistent approach to collective bargaining rights for employees of the public service is the C.C.F., whether at the provincial level or the federal level. However, late as it may be that support comes from other quarters, and even though that professed support is really not a policy of the party itself and perhaps exists only in the minds of a few individuals, nevertheless we welcome the attitude of those progressively-minded Liberals such as the hon. member for Hull who have finally come to the conclusion that perhaps collective bargaining is the only decent thing we can provide so far as employees in the public service are concerned.
I think it is also a fact that generally speaking over the years employees in the public service have from time to time been given rather shoddy treatment by governments in office. I think this has primarily been so because the employees have not had the right of determination, the right that other employees and other citizens in this country have, the right to participate in forming a union and in bargaining collectively with their employer.
I think this must be done. The only end to which we should look is to ensure that the employees in the public service of Canada, and in the various provinces, obtain the right to participate in shaping their own destiny. I believe it is of paramount importance that the law of the nation applying to the rights of individual employees to bargain collectively shall be equitably applied, so far as it is possible, to the employees in the public service.
I have dealt with this subject on other occasions in presenting the ideas I may have in bill form, Mr. Speaker, and I do not intend to go over the same ground again. I believe that each employee, whether he works in the 90205-6-1821
Civil Service Act
public service of Canada, a crown corporation or for a private concern, should be treated on an equal basis and should have the same rights, freedoms, responsibilities and opportunities, regardless of the particular group within which he may fall.
We can argue and quibble over details as to which system of collective bargaining may be more advantageous or more suited to a particular group of workers. We can say that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act should apply; that, with some alterations, we can establish a system of collective bargaining within the Civil Service Act; or we can say that we should set up some special law relating primarily to the employees of the public service. I do not believe it matters too much what the system is so long as it is a system based on equity, so long as we think in terms of treating the men and women in the public service of Canada on the same basis that we treat employees in private industry or in a crown corporation. I am referring to the right to work, along with your fellow workers, in negotiating with the employer to reach a mutually satisfactory collective agreement. I feel this is the only matter with which we should be concerning ourselves in so far as bargaining rights are concerned.
If there is no opportunity of obtaining a mutually satisfactory agreement within the framework of the system we would like to see, then I believe the parties should have the right to proceed to an outside agency for assistance and guidance or perhaps an arbitrary decision that would resolve the differences. The hon. member for Carleton mentioned what he and others have classified as bureaucratic patronage. There is no doubt that this is a very difficult form of patronage to put your finger on, Mr. Speaker, even more difficult than political patronage. If an individual finds he is subjected to bureaucratic patronage he has no opportunity now of finding a solution to this problem. I believe that when the parties are working out a collective agreement they should make provision for some grievance procedure, perhaps for some outside body to argue the case just as some individuals in industry do now.
The special committee to which this measure is going to be referred has a most important function in assessing and reviewing the subject matter of the bill referred to it. I for one hope that, as the parliamentary secretary indicated, this will be a non-partisan committee and that the government members of the committee will act as they individually think and as their consciences dictate after studying the bill. I hope they will not act, as has been the case so many

Civil Service Act
times in the past, as if they were mere puppets controlled by the Minister of Finance or some other government official.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words with respect to this legislation which is important, as everyone will agree because it deals with improvement of the Civil Service Act which is designed to give government employees a fair deal as befits a good employer. Unfortunately, it is a charter which falls short of giving the men and women working for the government, who have proved their loyalty and capabilities over a long period of years, the consideration which they richly deserve.
I am sure there is no division of opinion in the house when I say that we are fortunate in having a civil service second to none in the world. Where there is a division of opinion, however, is as to the way in which we treat these faithful servants who, in many instances, have refused better paying jobs in business and in industry so that they may carry on and remain at their posts.
Since the introduction of this measure I have listened with more than passing interest to the discussion of the merits of its content, and also of the ways in which it fails to meet the expectations of the civil service. I am particularly concerned with that part of the bill which ignores the fundamental rights of employees to negotiate with their employers in a manner recognized as a standard practice by the trades and labour movement of our country. It is true that it contains a reference to the right of initiating consultations but in no way does it recognize the right to negotiate an agreement; and in the event of disagreement there is no provision for the appointment of an arbitration board.
Speaking at a banquet of the Civil Service Association of Canada a year or so ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a statement which was generally understood to mean that the application of the principle of bargaining rights would be implemented in any future changes of the act. He said:
What is needed is more opportunity and better arrangement for your representatives to sit down at a table with officials representing the government and with officers of the civil service commission.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that what I have just read commits the Prime Minister to a measure which will recognize bargaining rights for all civil service employees.
Civil Service Act
A year ago last November the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) spoke at a mass rally of more than 1,000 federal government workers and took occasion to express the view that civil servants should have the right to negotiate with the government on salaries and working conditions. When he was asked if he would propose in parliament that these rights be granted, he replied that he would bring the matter up in the caucus of his party in order to obtain the views of his colleagues. I think he was sincere, but evidently he failed to convince the government that such a proposal was desirable or necessary.
In their submission the civil service association recommends that one of the clauses be amended to read as follows:
The cabinet or such ministers or minister or officer or officers of the crown it may designate, is empowered to negotiate directly and consult with representatives of appropriate associations and organizations or employees of the crown on all matters of personnel administration in the public service, including remuneration and all other terms and conditions of employment under regulations and procedures drawn under the provisions of this act. Such direct negotiations and consultations shall be initiated by the cabinet or its appointees on the one hand, and by recognized staff associations and organizations on the other hand.
I submit that such an amendment would not constitute the conferring of privileges not enjoyed by nearly all other employed workers, including those working in city hall staffs, firemen and policemen. The latter two categories enjoy all bargaining rights except for the fact that their contracts do not allow them to strike. However, they have the privilege if there is a break-down in negotiations of asking that the matter be considered by a board of arbitration whose decision will be binding on both sides. I am confident that the civil service association would not object to having such a clause added to this measure.
Professor Saul J. Frankel of McGill University, speaking at a gathering of the professional institute of the public service of Canada, made some very pertinent observations on the status of civil servants in Canada. He was speaking about the negotiation and arbitration system in Great Britain. After giving an outline of the history of the movement to obtain collective negotiation rights for civil servants, the professor stressed that the establishment of a collective negotiation body such as an arbitration board contributed a great deal toward better relations beween the government and civil servants. He made the statement that there is much less friction today than there was before they had such a right. Both sides agree to abide by the findings of the arbitration board and therefore there should be no fear that at

Civil Service Act
any time the government would be faced with civil servants going on strike.
Here we are primarily concerned with giving to a substantial and important segment of our people the same rights and privileges which other Canadians everywhere have taken for granted for more than 50 years. Let us ever be mindful of the fact that civil service employees, be they working in offices, government departments, income tax branches, as customs officials, immigration officers, whether they are serving on trains, steamships or in the far reaches of the north in humble but important tasks such as delivering the mail to our door, are giving their service to our government with loyalty and zeal irrespective of whether that government is Liberal or Conservative.
Of course, that is precisely what is expected of them, that they should serve no particular party but should simply perform their duties to the best of their ability and advise those in authority. Not the least of their functions is to counsel, because of their experience, on what may be best for the Canadian people.
I believe some dissension in the civil service is due to the fact that once an employee reaches the maximum salary for his particular position he must wait years before he can expect any salary increase. While it is true that civil servants may try examinations for a higher grade, it must be remembered that after ten or 15 years away from school the average man has forgotten much of the academic questions that appear on the usual civil service examination papers.
Although the civil servants may be able to step right into a better position and discharge his duties perfectly, he invariably finds himself teaching these duties to a student recently out of school. This student, by virtue of the fact that he still has the type of questions fresh in his mind, is usually able to pass the examination, whereas the older but much more experienced employee in the work actually required is often unable to pass. It has been the experience of some men to remain in the same salary bracket for 15 years and watch youngsters step out of school and into senior positions. In this case the older employee usually has to teach them the job.
At the present time it takes five years for a civil servant to reach his maximum salary rate. I wonder whether a plan could be evolved by which he would be kept in that position for another period of five years unless, of course, he successfully passed a higher examination at the end of this five-year period, so that he would automatically be promoted to a higher grade unless the head
[Mr. Badanal.l
of the department provided the commission with excellent reasons why he should not do so. Once promoted, the same routine would follow until five years prior to his retirement.
Such a plan would not only bring an end to much of the dissatisfaction in the service but would also increase its efficiency by giving civil servants an incentive in recognition of their efforts. I have in mind the case of an ex-secretary of the board of grain commissioners in the city of Fort William who was appointed secretary to the board when the statistician's office was moved to Winnipeg. This chap was a graduate of a university but had no experience. He lasted about a year. A local boy with a grade 11 education, who had started working in the office when he left school and had learned the practical end of the job by serving his apprenticeship over a period of years, took over the job and has been a success. In that particular job the university graduate was a failure.
There are many positions in the civil service in which a university education is not an essential ingredient for efficiency and which can best be filled by an older employee with years of experience. It seems to be an obsession in some quarters that unless one is a university graduate he should not aspire to top positions in the service. I realize, however, that there are positions for which a specialized university education is necessary. I am speaking primarily of the vast majority of the men and women in the service whose jobs have been learned by hard work and long hours over the years.
I now wish to mention a rather touchy subject, the restrictive discipline imposed upon civil servants with regard to their rights as citizens in connection with federal elections. One of the sections of this legislation does not provide security for an employee who may be dismissed because he had the temerity to enter the committee room of a candidate during an election or attended a political meeting. He may have to suffer the consequences of being cast into the ranks of the unemployed because of the whim of a member of a political party or perhaps the whim of a member of parliament.
I recall an instance during the 1958 federal election. A person in my constituency who held a position with the postal service told me he had been warned that if he took any part whatever in supporting my campaign he had better look for another job. This is by no means an isolated case.

In rising to take part in this debate I wish to open my remarks by expressing my appreciation of the objectivity which has been exhibited, generally speaking, by those hon. members who have preceded me. I think the general quality of the observations made so far has been of a very high order and I hope my own will not lower the standard in any respect.
I do not propose to go over the history of the legislation on this subject. That has been dealt with by other speakers. I think this legislation is a natural occurrence in relation to the developments of our times, bearing in mind that the original act was passed in 1918 and that great developments in government service, in these later years especially have made it necessary or desirable in the view of the former government and, now, of this government, that new legislation should be introduced. I was glad to see that the work put
Civil Service Act
in hand by way of an investigation by the chairman of the civil service commission was continued by the present government although it had been initiated by the former government. I am glad to see that the value of the report has been acknowledged and that legislation based at least in part upon that report has been brought forward.
There is one major point that concerns me with regard to this legislation. Under the present Civil Service Act the independence of the commission is made very clear. That independence is guaranteed in several ways, among others by the fact that the commissioners are appointed for a term certain as to tenure and can be removed only by the governor in council on a joint address by both houses of parliament. This guarantee goes to the very root of their independence. Moreover, they report not to a minister of the crown as such, but to parliament itself, the method of reporting being through a minister designated for that purpose.
For the last number of years the minister designated has been the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) and so far as I know there has been no change made in that procedure; at least, no change has been announced to the House of Commons. I am therefore a little curious to know why this legislation now before us is presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) rather than by the Secretary of State. My concern arises from what I regard as the absolute necessity of the commission remaining an independent body in line with the principle established in the former act. I hope it is nothing more than a matter of convenience, but perhaps the Minister of Finance would clarify the situation when he speaks.
If the hon. gentleman were to indicate that an attempt was being made to make the commission more directly answerable to the minister and I myself do not believe this is the case-it would, of course, give ground for real concern on all sides of the house. The minister has been accused on many occasions of bringing the C.B.C. too directly under his own influence because of his control over finance. While that may be a controversial point, I think it would be desirable for the minister to make it clear when he replies that there is no intention to take any steps to bring the commission more directly under ministerial authority. I may add that I see nothing in the legislation itself which would warrant such an inference, but I do think it is a point worthy of the hon. gentleman's attention.
In my opening remarks I made some reference to the speeches which had preceded mine on this second reading. I do want to except from that general statement the

Civil Service Act
remarks made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). In my view a great many of his remarks having to do with particular complaints were in the nature of superficial criticism of individual items rather than being addressed to the principles of the bill. Some of them, at least, contained what I considered to be rather poorly drawn innuendoes. They were points calculated to arouse passions and destroy pride in our civil service and our confidence in it.
In any event, I have no doubt-and it has been my experience-that in any large organization such as the civil service there are abuses from time to time. However, it seemed to me that the speech made by the hon. member did not address itself to the real problem. The problem before us is to enact the type of legislation which will enable such abuses to be corrected by the proper procedures for the relief of grievances and so on. In my view the purpose of this legislation is to provide methods by which such grievances can be remedied.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) began very well and made some excellent observations in the early part of his speech. In general he was handling the question in an exemplary way. Then he suddenly departed to that spiritual home of his, which I might call that segment of the people of the fine and historic riding he represents, Carleton Toryism. I do hope that he will not press those points in committee because, with deference to him, I suggest that some of them were quite historically inaccurate and not worthy of the earlier remarks he made in his speech.
If the hon. member will examine the text of his speech when it appears in Hansard, I think he will see that when he was speaking about the 1918 act he sought to claim that it was legislation brought about by, I think he used the term, the Conservative government of Sir Robert Borden. My reading of history rather indicated to me that the government headed by Sir Robert Borden at that time was a coalition government.

In any event, I wanted to check the hon. member on his history on that point and also to point out to him that in his reference to the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard), and the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), he was a little less precise than I think he would ordinarily wish to be in describing their speeches and the position they took. The speeches are on record and I do not propose to go over the points raised by them, but I do draw that matter to his attention and to the attention of the house in case anyone should take his version of the speeches as an accurate representation of the points discussed by them.
This bill is going to the committee and, while it is quite true one could raise a great many matters of principle that are debatable on second reading, I think it is desirable that these matters be discussed at the committee stage. I am concerned with one or two of the matters. At the time I was very critical of the handling by the Minister of Finance of the pay increases in 1959. As he well knows, there were different views on the techniques.

of his handling of those increases. I do not propose to repeat my criticism of his technique in handling that subject at that time, but I do wish to say that the difference of opinion and loss of confidence arising out of that episode indicated rather clearly the desirability of new legislation at least on that phase of the subject. I think probably the minister himself will agree with that. Indeed, the minister's remarks in presenting this legislation were considerably improved over some of the remarks he made at the time of the pay increases and his handling of that subject. I am quick to acknowledge that, Mr. Speaker. I think the Minister of Finance is entitled to have this said about his remarks so far on this bill.
In any event, the bill now presented does contain a very improved clause 7. I am quite sure that in committee this clause will get a rather thorough examination. It raises one aspect of the question of the technique or method of the public service organizations dealing with the government. While probably under the rules it is a matter that can properly be discussed on second reading, as far as I am concerned it can be better discussed in committee and I am quite prepared to reserve my remarks on it until that time arrives.
The necessity for the civil service bodies having the right to negotiate collectively, a right that is not something given to them at the whim, if you like, of the government but something established by law as their right is very important. That seems to be done by clause 7. Further aspects of it will have to be examined. There are different points of view on whether clause 7 does exactly what we think should be done, and there may be some shortcomings in it. In any event, it is not something that requires further debate here in principle.
Another matter which will require examination in committee is the some 25 or more changes between the bill introduced in the house last year and not proceeded with and the bill now before us. The reasons for some of the changes are readily apparent from reading them; others are not readily apparent and we shall expect to have detailed explanations of these matters in committee.
There is another point which was alluded to briefly by the hon. member for Carleton. It is rather well summed up in a report of the civil service commission of Canada dated December, 1958, commonly known as the Heeney report. While the hon. member did not quote it directly, he obviously had reference to this sentence which I shall read:
Not much is gained if the "malign influence" of political patronage is replaced by bureaucratic patronage which may be less apparent but which can be no less insidious and demoralizing.
Civil Service Act
All criticisms I have read of the proposed legislation and all analyses of it have raised this very point as something that will need careful examination in the new legislation. The rapidly developing extent of the civil service administration over the last few decades has undoubtedly required certain additional authority to be given administratively to deputy ministers within their own departments but that being so, there is a counterbalancing necessity of a strengthening of the procedure for any complaints about their administration. Great care will be required in the committee to make sure that the counterbalancing provisions in the bill now submitted are adequate and that they give civil servants who are subjected to the exercise of this added right by a deputy minister the right, if they feel aggrieved, to a proper appeal and proper remedial action.
The whole matter was dealt with at some length in what I thought was a very admirable analysis that appeared in the civil service association of Canada "Journal" for January 1961. The analysis dealt with two phases of last year's bill. The statement set forth was prepared by the national president in collaboration with the executive committee and the research advisory committee of the Civil Ser-ice Association of Canada. The legislation is dealt with generally and then there is a more detailed analysis in part 2 of the statement. I hope that when we get to the committee stage there will be an adequate opportunity when we are hearing the association's representatives to deal with the analysis point by point whether or not all the points are covered by particular clauses of the legislation.
I also hope there will be an adequate opportunity to examine the points that are included in the Heeney report and the appendices thereto, particularly some of the recommendations of that report which were not carried through into the legislation.
There is one other field that is of particular interest in discussing this subject. I have in mind the excellent development work which has taken place in the whole field of the relationship between the public service and government in Great Britain and more particularly the Whitley councils. Without spelling it out in legislation they seem to have evolved a technique of developing procedures that enables certain of these problems I have been discussing and other related ones to be dealt with in a way that is wholly desirable. I would hope that in the committee there will be an adequate opportunity to examine that technique in relation to our legislation.
In that connection I might point out that what I think is a rather interesting article has been prepared by Professor Frankel, who

Civil Service Act
is assistant professor in the department of economics and political science at McGill University and who made a study of the British civil service arbitration tribunal with a view to its possible adaptation to Canadian conditions. Interestingly enough, his research was made possible by a Canada council senior fellowship. I would hope that in the committee stage we can examine this whole subject in some detail with a view to its possible adaptation to conditions in Canada.
The other civil service associations all have their points of view, and while I have referred to the civil service association of Canada's analysis I do not want that to indicate any less interest in the comments and representations of the other civil service associations or public bodies which have dealt with this subject. I hope they can all be heard. I hope that when we come to the committee stage it will not be necessary to press this matter unduly but that we can find a technique of carrying on the work of the committee so that the hearings will be conducted expeditiously but at the same time will be full and thorough. I say that because it seems to me that under our system no government action can be fully effective without a thoroughly competent civil service to carry out policies as laid down by government and legislation as enacted by parliament.
We in Canada have been singularly well served over the years by our civil service. It has received praise from time to time and I think that praise has been well deserved. While some of the hon. members of the present government may not have expressed that praise as vigorously or as frequently as one might have wished when they first took office, it seems to me that in the last year or two they have come to appreciate our civil service. I was particularly pleased to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his opening remarks acknowledge the high standard of the civil service in the way he did and to hear him pay that compliment, if I may paraphrase his remarks, in the manner he did. Under our system we cannot afford to have a demoralized civil service or a civil service that is operating at less than peak efficiency. This is increasingly so as government inevitably reaches more and more into the affairs of private citizens as time goes on and as the decades pass.
Without saying more I should like to conclude by expressing my appreciation of the fact that this legislation has been introduced and by saying that I look forward with interest to serving on the committee which will examine the bill in a critical and, I hope, a very thorough and objective way.

If they check I think they will find that means have been found by both parties in Great Britain ever since 1919 to enable more and more British civil servants to take part in politics.
As I remember, the last figure I saw about a year ago was in a paper that had been prepared and which indicated that some
600,000	employees of the British government, especially those employed in what we would tend to call corporations or arsenals or other such establishments, are free to take part in politics and to belong to a political party. There is a continuing committee always examining various spots in the British civil service to determine when and where in the hierarchy a man reaches a position where it is felt that he can no longer take a free part in politics.
