speechtext: When he says they are permitted to become members of political parties, does that include standing for office?

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Yes, it very definitely does. In the last general election in Britain there were a number of people in all parties running for office who were government employees. A leave system is arranged. If a person wins he concludes his service, of course, but if he does not win then his leave is terminated and he goes back to the service. They have found great difficulty in delineating just what role a man may have within the civil service before he is free to take part in political activities.
As I look around this house, and I have expressed this view before, I find about 100 lawyers, a great many small businessmen, a great many farmers and a few teachers. I have been able to find only two hon. members who, you might say, come from large scale corporate organizations. I refer to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and the hon. member who sits next to him, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). In other words, this house lacks

representation from the large corporate organizations that dominate our business and financial life. At the same time, as I am sure every hon. member knows who has been around a university, a great deal of our best talent is funnelled off into the civil service.
I wonder how much longer we can go on depriving politics of the ability that lies in these two areas, that is to say the very able people who go into the. civil service and the very able people who go into corporate organizations.
I know there is no law that says someone who is an executive in a corporate organization cannot run for office, but in the main they do not. They take very little part in politics. This reference, of course, is outside the scope of the debate, but the civil service aspect of it is not. I think it is about time we began to be large enough in spirit, as the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) suggested, to consider this possibility instead of being petty. I know that I had a shock several years ago when I discovered that if a member of parliament made a complaint about a civil servant taking part in political activities, that pretty well sunk the civil servant. This was the accepted Canadian practice. At the time, the Minister of Transport pointed out he was merely following the practice of the preceding administration.
I cannot honestly say that if the members of the civil service were able to take part in political activity and belong to a party, it would do me or my party any particular good. I would say, judging from the political attitude of the provincial civil servants in our part of the country, that most of them would be Conservative. So far as I am concerned, that is fine. I would be agreeable to their taking part in party activities so long as those activities remained within a certain level and did not have an effect on policy decisions.
The second point upon which I should like to touch is not a very popular one with some of my colleagues and, I imagine, with other hon. members of the house. However, this is a personal observation, and I feel I should reiterate it at this time. I feel that there should be much more leeway to bring people in from the outside to fill top positions in the civil service. It seems to me that one of the feelings I often encounter in government- I do not think I am giving anything away- is the feeling that senior civil servants may not be as enthusiastic as they might be about their minister and the things he wants to do. I believe this is unfair, not only to this government but to any government. For that reason, I should like to see much more-not so much of heads rolling at the top-of the practices followed when a minister takes office of surrounding himself with his own
Civil Service Act
people. I do not mean the executive assistants, I mean the senior posts in the department. I believe that the civil service commission and the act should be so set up that the minister could do this.
I would point out to hon. members that such a provision would do two things. It would mean we were developing in Canada the idea of a new cabinet bringing in its own experts to help it with its policy direction and, second, it would eliminate the excuse I have heard so often, "Well, how do you expect us to get things going when so many of the civil servants are against us?" I do not believe the civil servants are against the government and I would not like to make that point. However, I do believe we have a lot of time servers and quite a bit of dead-wood at the top of the civil service because of the conditions of employment. If I were a minister I would want to have a little bit of room-enough space at the top-so I could fill it with people who were dedicated, not only to me and the policy I wanted to introduce but also to the subject of the field itself.
Now, as I said, this may sound like heresy but I feel that if we had more of this type of thing we would have much more life and dynamics not only in the civil service but also in the government of Canada. In this particular case, I think we can look to both the United States and British examples and see the way they take advantage of drawing on people on the outside. It seems to me a rather invidious commentary upon the party that took power three years ago that they brought in only one deputy minister. They actually brought him in as an assistant deputy minister but as a result of a death he moved up. Surely, the Conservative party had close to it or within it more people of ability that they wanted to have help them guide the country along with some sense of direction. I am not speaking as a Conservative. I am trying to speak as someone who would like to see some real sense of direction within the administration. As it is now, with our present civil service setup, it seems to me that governments pass on but civil servants go on forever. I am wondering if this is not one of the reasons that I, as an opposition member, feel this government has not had the dynamics and drive one might have expected from it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I should like to thank all hon. members for the support they have expressed for this government measure, which evidently has gained support in all parts of the house. I do thank all hon. members for the support they have indicated. I had not intended to participate in the debate by way of reply, Mr. Speaker, but certain points have been raised, and in particular by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mc-Ilraith), who directed several inquiries to me with which he asked me to deal before the debate is closed.
Most of the matters that have been raised in the course of the debate can be dealt with more conveniently in the committee. Perhaps, however, I might touch on several of these at this time in closing the debate on second reading.
The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) indicated in his remarks that he is under the impression that civil servants appearing before appeal boards are not permitted to have counsel. If this is the view of the hon. member, I must tell him he is labouring under a misapprehension, because civil servants are entitled to be represented by counsel in appearing before appeal boards. Indeed, this is the practice in Ottawa, and some of the most eminent counsel at the Ottawa bar appear from time to time before appeal boards on behalf of civil servants.
The individual matter which perhaps engaged most attention of hon. members participating in the debate, concerned the provision in the bill providing for consultation with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees with respect to pay and other terms and conditions of employment.
This provision is for consultation, of course, at the request of such representatives as well as at the instance of either the civil service commission or the Minister of Finance.

I have no doubt that this provision will continue to receive attention when it is before the committee and I do not intend to dwell at length upon it.
I made some observations on the general tenor of the bill in introducing it on Tuesday. However, I should perhaps draw attention to one fact that evidently has been overlooked by some hon. members. We have heard a good deal of praise of the Heeney report and properly so. In speaking on Tuesday I had occasion to pay tribute to this really outstanding report. Nevertheless I invite hon. members to consider the fact that the Heeney report did not recommend collective bargaining. Indeed, the Heeney report did not recommend any provision going as far as the provisions of this bill go. Let me remind hon. members of exactly what it was that is said on this subject in the Heeney report. I am referring now to paragraph 32 of the report under the heading of "employee participation". It reads as follows:
The commission believes that in the general interest, means should be developed to enable civil servants to participate more effectively in the process by which their salaries and conditions of work are determined. We note that the Prime Minister during the past year had occasion to make reference to the government's interest in improvement in this respect. We have concluded that the differences in the circumstances of private and public employment do not readily admit of the simple and unqualified application to the civil service of the normal industrial pattern of collective bargaining. Nevertheless, we believe that, by developing and enlarging the role of the commission in this area and by strengthening the National Joint Council, it should be possible, with the co-operation of the staff associations, to arrive at a solution which would meet the essential objectives of the employees without involving the genuine difficulties associated with other proposals.
The outline of such a solution is contained in appendix "B" to this report. It is recommended that, if this proposal meets with government's approval, the commission be requested to develop and institute suitable machinery and procedures to give effect thereto, in consultation with treasury board and senior departmental officials on the one hand and the principal staff organizations on the other. The commission has had in mind the possibility of such development in its review of existing legislation, but we have concluded that it is neither necessary nor desirable that detailed provisions on this subject should be embodied in the law.
Mr. Speaker, I now turn to appendix (b) of the report where in some detail the civil service commission outlines what is called "general consultation between government and employees on pay and conditions of work". There the three members of the commission have indicated in some 12 paragraphs their views on this subject, and they conclude with two recommendations which are as follows:
We therefore recommend:
(a) That the government request the civil service commission, in consultation, with officials of treasury

board and other departments on the one hand, and the staff associations on the other, to develop and institute procedures along the lines described above for the participation of government employees in the determination of levels of compensation in the civil service, and
(b) That, in consultation with the civil service commission, the National Joint Council be requested to examine its constitution and terms of reference, and to submit recommendations to government for making it more useful and effective as a forum of joint consultation in other matters of mutual concern.
The type of collective consultation which the three commissioners there recommended was one in which, as has been described, the civil service commission would sit at the end of a table in a somewhat detached capacity, the representatives of the civil service organizations and associations would sit on one side and representatives of the treasury board would sit on the other, and there would be discussions. This report had barely been made public when at least some of the civil service associations expressed themselves quite forcibly on the subject and indicated that this kind of system did not meet with their views. While there were discussions of that matter, it was made quite clear from the outset that these proposals did not go far enough to meet the views of the representatives of the civil service organizations and associations. I say no more on that subject at this time except to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the bill now before the house in this regard goes substantially farther than did the commissioners in their recommendations in the Heeney report.
The next point which perhaps should be mentioned now, Mr. Speaker, is the one for which the hon. member for Port Arthur argued vigorously. He evidently believes that civil servants should be free of all restrictions in the matter of participation in political activities. Evidently he does not stop short of believing that all trammelling restrictions upon civil servants in that regard should be forthwith abolished. This view has not prevailed in the House of Commons and I doubt that it will commend itself to most hon. members.

speechtext:
No; I meant the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai). I thank the hon. member from Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) for the correction.
The act at the present time is quite specific on this subject. Section 55 of the present act reads as follows:
Civil Service Act
55. (1) No deputy head, officer, clerk or employee in the civil service shall be debarred from voting at any dominion or provincial election if, under the laws governing the said election, he has the right to vote; but no such deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with any such election, or contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for any party funds.
(2) Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be dismissed from the civil service.
The one change that the present bill would make in that existing provision of the Civil Service Act is to provide that no person shall be dismissed for violation of this provision unless the alleged violation has been the subject of an inquiry at which that person has been given the opportunity of being heard. The new bill ameliorates the provisions in this respect to that extent but it maintains -and, I submit, properly so-the prohibition of political activities on the part of civil servants.
The hon. member for Fort William can complain about this matter if he wishes to do so, as being an interference with the personal rights of a citizen in a free country. However, the fact remains that larger issues are involved here. There is involved the whole question of the public interest; and the public interest has been served by a civil service which has been denied the right to take part in partisan politics. How can you expect a civil service to earn the kind of respect, the kind of approbration which has been expressed frequently in the course of this debate; a civil service that can equally serve succeeding governments regardless of changes in political stripe of governments, that can give the same service to a successor government it gave to the predecessor if the civil service on the one hand is going to be permitted to engage in political activities or, on the other hand, is going to be exposed to them?
There is an element in this situation that has evidently been overlooked by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai). It is the extent to which provisions of this kind protect the civil service. This is something of simply overriding importance. If the civil service did not enjoy the protection of a prohibition of this kind, those who are engaged in the civil service would be open to all kinds of pressures, or could be submitted to all kinds of pressures by any government in office.
In days gone by, long years ago, when our parliamentary system was growing up, measures of this kind would have been of very great protection to the civil service. Measures of this kind were not introduced simply to impose some arbitrary restriction upon the

Civil Service Act
political rights of individuals. They were imposed, first, in order that the public interest might be better served by those who can under all circumstances give equal loyalty to successive governments regardless of political stripe. In the second place, the civil service itself should be protected under all circumstances from pressures exerted upon it by whatever government happened to be in power, or by the party that happened to be out of power if it sought to bring pressure to bear on the civil service to help them win their way into power.
That is the reason for a prohibition of this kind on political activities, so that no civil servant can be dragooned by his minister into taking part in political activities or called upon to make any contribution to party funds. Let us see this in its proper light. It is not an interference with political rights; it is a matter of giving effective protection to the public service against all kinds of subtle pressures that might otherwise be exerted upon it by a government that did not have too many scruples in that respect. I say nothing more on that subject.
I turn next to the matter that was touched upon by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), namely the numerous changes that appear in the present bill as compared with Bill No. C-77 introduced last June at the 1960 session of parliament. I do not propose to repeat what I said on this subject in moving second reading on March 7. What I said in this regard is to be found in Hansard at pages 2760 and 2761. I drew attention to the fact that there are many changes between the two bills, most of them of a minor nature relating to administrative questions.
However, there are two changes of a quite material nature. These are changes in policy and I outlined them at that time. I do not wish to dwell on this subject, but there is a complete misinterpretation of my remarks on this subject appearing in the Ottawa Journal of March 8 at page 21. This is the sentence:
Of the many changes in the Civil Service Act contemplated in this bill, said Mr. Fleming, most are "of a minor and administrative significance only".
What I had to say about changes of minor and administrative significance only was with regard to the changes between Bill No. C-77 introduced last June and the present measure. If you compare this measure with the Civil Service Act, you will find that there are many changes, and I think there are enough of them to engage the serious study of the proposed committee for some period of time.
A point was sought to be made that this measure is introduced in the name of the

Minister of Finance and not in the name of the Secretary of State. Perhaps I should feel flattered that this should be regarded as a matter worthy of comment by some hon. gentlemen opposite. The fact is that under our existing system of government the Secretary of State answers to the house for the estimates of the civil service commission, but all matters pertaining to pay, salary, working conditions and terms of employment are, and have been for a long time, matters for which the Minister of Finance is held responsible.
Ever since I have been in the house, since 1945, this has been the division of responsibility. My predecessors, Mr. Ilsley, Mr. Abbott and Mr. Harris were the spokesmen of the government in the house for all matters pertaining to salaries, working conditions and terms of employment of the civil service. It has been my privilege in these past three years and eight months to introduce in the house those changes which have been, I trust, of great benefit to the civil service, namely the increases in salaries-

I have on the order paper a motion, which will be called immediately after the bill has been given second reading, to establish a committee for that particular purpose. When agreement has been reached among the parties as to the personnel of that committee, it will be appointed and the bill can then be formally referred to the committee for study and report.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the house for the support which those who have participated in this debate have indicated for the measure. I believe it to be a measure of very high importance. Indeed I regard it as one of the most important bills likely to come before this present parliament. I look forward with some degree of gratification to seeing a strong committee appointed which will give this bill a very, very thourough study.
The committee, of course, will be master of its own procedure. It will, if it wishes, be entitled to call on and hear representatives of the civil service organizations and associations and to give the bill a most thorough scrutiny. I believe its importance warrants nothing short of a very thorough scrutiny. I can tell hon. members, having had some experience of scrutinizing this measure in its preparation and the study of the Heeney report that preceded it, that it is a very large subject. But in a matter of this kind the extent of the study on the part of hon. members both in the house and in the committee will be repaid, I believe, by the satisfaction they will derive from dealing with a subject of such great importance to good government in Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kenora-
Rainy River says "hear, hear" and he is quite right.
I want to say that in this instance certain facts were made available by the person himself on a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation national program and were used as the basis of a broadcast. In so doing this person removed the veil of secrecy and confidence, if there was any, surrounding his employment record. In view of that, Mr. Chairman, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Cariboo is as follows:
Can the Minister of Labour tell the house the circumstances of Mr. Glen Exelby, who was depicted in the main role of the C.B.C. program "Close-Up" last night, and inform the house whether the national employment service is doing anything to secure employment for him?
I repeat, in view of the fact that Mr. Exelby had made most of the information available, there was no secrecy attaching to his employment record. I supplemented that record by saying that he first registered for employment at the national employment office on September 9. I went on to say:
He had quit his previous employment as a salesman at $6,000 per year and had given the reason that there was "no future".
There is no secrecy about that. I continue:
On November 29 he was referred as a salesman at $350 per month to Service Steel and Engineering in Hamilton.
There is no secrecy about that. He answered an advertisement put out by the C.B.C. requesting a white collar worker for a television program. There is no secrecy about that. I continue:
Supply-Labour
Apparently he was successful in obtaining this employment and I am informed that it was remunerative to the extent of $25 per day.
There is no secrecy about that. As a matter of fact, he earned $50 a day. My reply continued:
On February 24 the unemployment insurance commission office in Hamilton offered Mr. Exelby a position as a foreman at Frost Metal Products-
There is no secrecy about that, nor is there any secrecy about anything in the reply I made to the question asked by the hon. member for Cariboo. I further said, as recorded in Hansard of March 9, at page 2810, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Welland, as follows:
Is it possible for the Minister of Labour to procure information regarding the employment record of a person registered with the national employment service if he is requested to do so by a member of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I think it is evident that the hon. member for Welland refers to the reference I made yesterday in respect to Mr. Exelby.
To that, as I looked at the hon. member for Welland, who is now in his seat, he nodded agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I said:
If that is so, Mr. Speaker, then I feel that if Mr. Exelby undertook of his own volition to disclose his personal affairs in great detail on a national television broadcast and in so doing created a completely false impression, it is quite proper for me to present certain facts of the same nature.
I should like to refer also to my original statement in answer to the hon. member for Cariboo which I completed by saying:
I am very sorry that the program did not reveal these facts also-
-since they were evidently in the process of revealing all of the employment facts of this person in question.
Now, the charge of breaking the law, of course, enters the realm of the foolish and has existence only in the inflamed imagination of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate, and I am sorry that he is not present at this time. But this is not the first time that a charge of this nature has been levelled. It is a favourite gambit of the hon. member for Essex East, and I do not believe we have to look any further than that for the

Supply-Labour
origin of this charge. It is a charge which he made last year with relation to the administration of the unemployment insurance fund and now it has been resurrected and trotted out to do its duty once again on behalf of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The statement which I made last May, Mr. Chairman, covers the situation fully.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. The minister asked that he not be interrupted and I have acceded to his request. He stated that he wanted to make a statement and has proceeded to do so but in the making of that statement he has now charged motives to the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, both of whom are away on important business.
The question of privilege I raise is that the minister complains about the fact that he has been unfairly treated and that unfair charges have been levelled against him but he is doing exactly the same thing with reference to the hon. member for Essex East, who did not raise the question, and also with reference to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who did raise the matter by way of a question on orders of the day and also in the debate. My question of privilege is that it seems to me the minister should not proceed in the manner that he complains members on this side of the house have adopted against him.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had finished making charges, as the hon. member for Laurier wishes to describe them. However, I must point out that I sat here yesterday and had to listen to many falsehoods and charges which were made last evening.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: They were not falsehoods any more than the statement the minister has made now.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
The statement I made last May covered the situation fully. I indicated my intention at that time of making available to members of parliament and also to members of provincial legislatures information existing in the files of the unemployment insurance commission. There was not a word of objection at that time from anyone sitting on the opposition benches. That statement still stands. This is my policy, Mr. Chairman, and it has been my policy ever since.
Let me point out also that as Minister of Labour I have every right to set such a policy. I had every right in May of 1960 to say that I would make information available to members of parliament. I had every right to make such information available in
[Mr. Starr.l
answer to the question of the hon. and respected member for Cariboo on Wednesday. I also had every right to do what I did last May, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knew very well at that time and as he knew very well last night when he was making his trumped-up charge.
I remind him and other members of the committee of subsection 5 of section 22 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. This is the section dealing with the employment service. Subsection 5 of section 22 reads as follows:
The commission is responsible to the minister in respect of the administration of this part.
There is no question of interpretation here, Mr. Chairman, no twisting and turning such as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate indulged in last night when he attempted to interpret section 98. Section 22 gives the minister full authority in the administration of the employment service and the information supplied to the house was information solely and completely relating to employment, over which the minister has full authority.
As a matter of fact, the gentleman in question was not registered for benefits because his salary in his former job was above the insurable ceiling. The information in question is information that is given out to employers every day right across this country. Does anyone think you can operate an employment service and refer claimants to jobs without telling the employer where they last worked, how much they earned and so on? It is also information which had already been made known through the television screens of the nation but in a form that was far from complete.
Why are hon. members objecting to setting the record straight? The answer to that is quite obvious. They do not want the record to be set straight. The hon. member for Essex East suggested today that an injustice had been done to the gentleman in question. Let me assure him that nothing was further from my mind. The only injustice done has been that hon. members of the opposition have sought to make a political football of the gentleman in question, and nobody deplores these tactics more than I do.
I put certain facts on the record because 1 thought that as a matter of public interest they should go on the record. There was no intention of injuring any person. It was a matter of setting the record straight and that is all.
Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that if the facts had been fully presented on the television program to which I have referred it would not have been necessary to present the full facts in this chamber. However, once a picture had been presented and that picture was

incomplete it became a duty to present a full picture, and this was done. To say that there was anything wrong in this is, I submit, just sniveling nonsense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: The minister said he would answer questions after he sat down and I did not want to interrupt him because of his request. I would ask the minister what distinction he makes between the information which he divulged to the house in connection with this matter and information which might be divulged to a member of parliament concerning the income tax return of an individual?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: There is a great deal of difference. I want to point out again to the hon. member for Laurier what I said on May 19, 1960, as reported on page 4033 of Hansard. I want to repeat it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: I would appreciate an answer to the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
There is a great deal of difference in this particular case. I said then:
. .. any member of this house will be given whatever information he requests, provided that the information is available and that it is not of a confidential or privileged nature.
I say that the difference in this particular case is that the gentleman in question revealed his employment picture of his own volition over the television system of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and that since he did that and made public his employment record there was no secrecy involved in setting the record straight and giving the full picture with regard to his employment record.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: I thank the minister for that reply but it leads me to this question. Once the veil of secrecy has been lifted in regard to a matter of this kind, even though it concerns the income tax return of an individual, does the minister say that a matter of that nature should be revealed to a member of parliament or to anybody else?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: I think that is putting the question on an altogether different basis. The two situations have nothing in common. If the employment record, as I pointed out, is not confidential or privileged, it can be revealed. If it is, then it cannot. In this particular instance, the veil of secrecy was lifted by the individual himself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I will not be long in dealing with this matter but there are one or two questions to which I should like the minister to reply. Do I understand the minister correctly, if an individual lifts the veil of secrecy on a matter such as that to which he has referred-I am putting aside for the moment
Supply-Labour
the income tax return-then, the minister has every right, notwithstanding section 98, to give that information publicly?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: Well, in so far as an employment record is concerned there is not that same sense of secrecy at all because employers right across this country have access to information in employees' records. It is the only basis upon which many of them are prepared to hire people. There is not that same sense of secrecy or confidential nature as there may be in any other matter. The matter of an employment record is not secret to that same extent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
The minister has made a statement about giving it to an employer. Well, giving it to an employer is one thing, but giving it publicly is an entirely different thing and it is contrary to section 98.
I come back to the original question: Does the minister take the view that in the statement which he made he was not in contravention of section 98?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: Yes. There is nothing in my statement of March 8 regarding the employment record of the man in question that is a contravention in any shape or form.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: One last question: Is the minister now going to make public the personal details of an applicant for unemployment benefits?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: That depends on the circumstances of each case.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if he would be willing to make available to me or any other hon. member of the committee the information he made available to the hon. member for Cariboo concerning an applicant registered in the national employment service?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: The hon. member has access, by virtue of the rescinding of a directive in respect of these matters, to any information that is available at a local office.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I was the gentleman who asked the question. I saw the film and I was not altogether satisfied. My wife was awake all night because she was crying most of the night about the sobsister who had been on that film. I said, "I will find out in the morning when I go to parliament whether or not this is genuine." This fellow should have had a job with D. W. Griffith, and she could have worked for those two actresses we saw on Sunday. She was just as good a sobsister.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
May I ask one further question? In answer to a question I put to the

Supply-Labour
minister as to a representative of the national employment service taking part in the program, he said he did not know. Has the minister inquired and can he tell the committee whether he has ascertained the facts?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: Yes, I have made inquiries and the officials of the national employment service office in Hamilton inform me that they saw no script and knew nothing of what was going to be in the script.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to ask a question, I shall yield the floor to him.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the hon. member for Laurier, and it is this: It seems to me we have to take a common sense view of this case as put by the hon. member for Cariboo a moment ago. We are really ignoring the important effects of what was done. As a result of what took place the other night, a very large number of people in this country, beginning with the wife of the hon. member for Cariboo, have been distressed beyond words. I think a disservice has been done to the whole situation. It so happens that I have a daughter who is a social worker and I know how deeply these people are affected by the distressing cases that come before them.
In reviewing what has happened we have to have common sense. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to whom I usually listen with great respect, was away below his usual level the other night. I wish he were here today because he is the kind of man who, when he is wrong, will say so. As I say, he was away below his usual level in sneering at the minister. He almost went so far as to say that we on this side were not sympathetic to the unemployed.
In so far as disclosing information is concerned, surely what happened was that Exelby by going on the air, created a situation in which, in the interests of truth and of the facts of life the minister almost had to come to this house and state the truth. I gravely question the judgment of the C.B.C. in this case. When the hon. member accuses the minister of behaving improperly, he seems to me to be ignoring the common sense view. If there was-even the slightest technical irregularity-and apparently there was not, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate appeared to suggest that the minister should have communicated with the board instead of with the representative in Hamilton. Does anyone suggest that if the minister had communicated with the board he would not have secured the information?
Further, let me say a word on the legal aspects of this matter. In law, there are two sides to a question; there is equity as well

as law. I suggest that if there is the slightest technical irregularity from the point of view of a breach of the law, which I doubt, from the point of view of equity what the minister did was justified over and over and over again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I do not want to be drawn
into a debate on this matter, and I do not intend to be. However, I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood would not object if I did make just one or two comments on what he has said.
In the first place, I do not believe anybody will disagree with the statement that many people were distressed by what they saw and what they heard. I also want to add that many people were distressed by what the minister said in the house.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
Just a moment; I hope I will be allowed to say what I intend to say. I am not charging the minister with having made a statement that did not come from the officers of the unemployment insurance. I think what the minister did was to give the house the information which he received from his own officers. On that point, I do not believe there can be any doubt; that is not charging any insincerity to the minister.
What I do say is this, sir. If it was distressing to hear that one story it was equally distressing to hear the other from the minister and because of this event, if any other occasion arises, not necessarily on television but in some other medium such as the press, the minister may get up and give information which is of a confidential nature, and whether it be on an equitable or on a legal basis will make absolutely no difference. The point is this: Was it legal and was it authorized under section 98 or was it not? The contention we are making is that it was not authorized.
I know what the hon. member for Greenwood would say about an infraction of the law if he were sitting on this side of the chamber. I clearly remember one occasion when the minister of justice in another administration was charged with having broken the law because he had not complied with one section of an act having to do with the administration of a board or commission which came within his jurisdiction.
There was no end of attack on the minister of justice at that time because he had broken the law. There is no doubt that there has been an infraction of the law in this case. It will not serve the purpose for the hon. member for Greenwood to say that, although the law has been broken, in equity this is the

way in which it should be treated. It will be for parliament to decide that matter and for others as well.
Let me make one final point. The hon. member for Greenwood said that it was important that the truth be told. I would not for one moment stand here and say that the minister has not told the truth. The point is that the person in question, namely, Exelby, has denied at least one if not two of the statements to a reputable newspaper and has said that the statement made by the minister as given to him by officers of his department is untrue. I therefore say to the hon. member for Greenwood that the truth has not been established. It may well be that some of the statements made to the press by Exelby were not accurate. I simply wanted to rise not so the Minister of Labour will think that I am accusing him but rather to say that I realize that he gave information that came from his own officers; and I repeat, whether in equity or whether in law, it was in breach of the statute and should not be allowed.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: Let us clear up the matter in the committee on industrial relations.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: May I put a question to the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: The hon. member for Peterborough has the floor.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I was hoping to begin my remarks on the estimates of the Department of Labour by offering congratulations to the national employment service, and I still wish to do so. I have a good deal to do with officials of the national employment service. I have found them to be most kindly and most effective in their work. One of the things about which I have been most happy is the fact that employees of the national employment service have not begun to act as they *did back in the thirties when there was large scale unemployment and to treat workers who came to them with an air of superiority. I have had much experience with the operations of the employment service and I think it is something for which the Minister of Labour can be congratulated.
However, this is the particular problem which I see in this whole situation before us. I would not go as far as to say that the minister has broken the law. However, I would say that he has committed an indiscretion. He has lowered public opinion across this nation of the national employment service employee. I wonder whether people who go into these offices are not going to be rather concerned about giving personal information to these employees, fearing lest the facts disclosed may be made public on the floor of the house, through newspapers or any other
Supply-Labour
medium. I think we have reached the nub of this whole problem. I congratulate the Minister of Labour on the fact that he changed the directive which would not have allowed members of parliament to obtain information. Surely, members of parliament, when going to national employment service employees and asking for information, regard that information as confidential; and surely people at the local national employment service offices in giving information are not going to expect that their member is going to march into that office, find out some pertinent information and then spread it across the local press. If I believed that, I think members of parliament would go into the national employment service offices on a number of occasions which would embarrass this government. The tragedy of this matter is not that what Mr. Exelby said in front of the television camera was evidently or seemingly untrue. The tragedy is that it has brought disrepute on people who are suffering. If the C.B.C. had looked far enough, I am sure they could have found other people.

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext: Why did they not do so?

maintopic: PACIFIC PRESS LIMITED-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF INVESTIGATION
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BILL NO. C-71
speechtext:
I am sorry but I have nothing to do with the C.B.C. I would also suggest that the C.B.C. should bear the brunt of this particular criticism. Perhaps at the same time as I say that I should say that we in a sense have created the situation because the unemployed have a fierce pride. They went through the forties and the fifties believing that unemployment would never come to them, that they were living in a democratic state in an economy that would never let them down, that unemployment insurance would see them through. They do not want to go in front of television cameras except, evidently, people like Mr. Exelby.
I know that we have a local board which tries to find the facts about unemployed families, to get the facts from people who are unemployed. What happens? They could not find one single person who would open his mouth. I have heard people say "Where are your unemployed?" We do not see lineups of unemployed on the street. No, they are not on the street. They believe that the day of soup kitchens and line-ups by reason of unemployment are over. This government gave them reason to believe that they were over in the election campaign of 1957 and 1958.
No, we do not have to blame the national employment service. That was not the reason why the statement was made. We have a grave situation for the national employment service. I say that the Minister of Labour went much farther than was necessary. He

Supply-Labour
was asked about the circumstances of Mr. Exelby. The circumstances had nothing to do with what Mr. Exelby said to his former employer when he left the service of that employer, when he said there was no future in this particular line of work as advertising agent or whatever it was; that is the real tragedy.
This is what I am wondering about. We are entering into an era of more and more government concern or more and more government planning. This will depend upon more and more information being given by individuals and corporations. Are we going to lose all concern for the rights of people who give information that can be passed on to others who need that information, such as the record of an employee given to a future employer? Are we not going to be in a position where people will be afraid to give information because of what may appear the next day on television or in the newspapers? Have we lost all interest in and all concern for the individual rights of people in this nation? Are we becoming so thin skinned as a government that we cannot now see anything on television without concern?
Are we going to have people standing up complaining every time there is a C.B.C. play about fishermen? Are we going to have the Minister of Fisheries stand up and tell us that because the hold was only half full it does not really give the picture of fishing on the west coast? Are we going to have this continual defence of everything coming out of television and through the public press? Are we going to have a full scale investigation of individuals who put on interviews for the C.B.C.? Are our skins getting so thin as that? Or is it the thought that parliament is so great that we are overlooked and we now have to defend, whether it is television broadcasts or newspaper reports.

I think the Department of Labour is going to be one of the most difficult departments in the government with which to concern oneself in the years to come. Mr. James S. Band, deputy minister of welfare for the province of Ontario has suggested that in the next decade automation is going to replace four out of five industrial workers. We do not seem to be able to do anything about our problem of seasonal employment. We realize that every four years we have a period of cyclical unemployment and every time this gets worse. There is a greater number of unemployed after

each of these depressions and recessions, and in fact we never really fully recover from them.
Looking at the estimates of the Department of Labour I cannot see that this department is really facing up to this situation. As hon. members of the official opposition have suggested, this government has not recognized it as a national emergency. I think what we need in this country is a full realization that this is our No. 1 problem. I think we should have a meeting or conference, something on the scale of the Gordon commission, to look at this problem facing our nation and to ascertain what the unemployment situation is going to be over the next ten or 20 years. It should not be just an economic survey but a full scale inquiry concerned with the problem of unemployment. I realize that other surveys are going on, but surely we could project our plans and commitments over the next five or ten years and give this government or whatever government is in power some idea of what is necessary to solve the problem.
Before we can do anything, surely we have to recognize what is going to develop in this country over the next five or ten years. I am convinced that winter works programs, which were a drop in the bucket last year and are this year two drops in the bucket, are not going to be a solution to this problem. The minister suggested that 200,000 jobs were provided by the winter works program, but in one particular constituency, my own, these jobs were on a six weeks' basis. They tried to pass the jobs around to as many people as possible. Does the figure of 200,000 people employed on winter works programs include those people who had just six weeks' work? If that is the basis on which this number was computed, perhaps that is an area where we should have an actual break-down in the number of jobs, the number of people who tok those jobs and the length of time for which they were employed.

Thank you very much. I must have missed that. As I say, to consider work on the winter works program is, I think, completely irrelevant. Too often it was not work that had to be done. There is also confusion here which I think is very important affecting the Department of Labour. That is the confusion between work and welfare. Until we in this country gain some respect for work and labour I am afraid we are never going to be able to compete with other countries in the world in our development. One of the
Supply-Labour
things I have come to dislike about the winter works program is the fact that too many jobs are being carried out. In other words, we have the men digging somewhere when that work could be done by a bulldozer with one man. We employ ten men with picks and shovels simply because that way we will employ an extra nine men rather than put them on the welfare lists. Perhaps that is a good thing. In other ways it is not a good thing because I do not think any man has much respect for the service he is giving to his community when he knows he is being employed simply because the government does not want to give him a hand-out in some other way.
This is not the answer to the kind of economic problems we are going to have over the next five or ten years. Even the winter works projects were restrictive. I know one community which wanted to acquire an area for industrial redevelopment. This was not allowed. This was the kind of job which could have been done and in connection with which men could have been employed. But the program was too restrictive and as a result the project was not allowed under the winter works program.
Also, I think that leaving it to the municipalities is not the way to deal with this problem. The municipalities are overburdened with their own problems and the costs of overseeing the whole project are far too great for them. The responsibility should not be left to them.
I should now like to turn to another phase of the estimates of the Department of Labour. I refer to the retraining scheme brought in last session. I supported this retraining scheme with considerable enthusiasm at the time the legislation was brought in. However, I must say that my enthusiasm has been dampened over the last few weeks because I have failed to see anything very dynamic being done in the scheme.
I should like to repeat the words of the Minister of Labour quoted in a news release put out by his department. The minister said:
We are now in a period when we can no longer afford the luxuries of indifferent preparation and use of our manpower resources.
Local school boards and departments of education find it difficult to work adequately in the light of national needs. Business and industry work within their own interests. Without some co-ordinated planning and effort beyond what can be given by ten different school systems considerable confusion will probably be our lot.
Is not that exactly what we have done? The federal government has taken no more responsibility in this regard than simply handing money to the provinces, who in turn have handed it to the municipalities.

Supply-Labour
What kind of co-ordination do we have on that basis? The minister went on to say:
We are in competition with nations of the world where the development of human resources is planned on a broad scale. In these countries the development of manpower potential is given a high priority and technical and vocational training is a continuing process from school through years of employment.
That is the very point. There is no national co-ordination. We do not know where we are going. When a group of unemployed people desire a retraining scheme-and I congratulate them for their enthusiasm-the local municipalities have to deal with the matter. They are interested in the program, but they are also overburdened with their own problems. This is no help to a group of people who have been working hard in one job and want to work hard in another.
Then there is this point. How do the municipalities know what are the national needs? They simply look for something which seems to fit, and you have municipalities training welders when there are already welders on the streets looking for work. If for the next ten years the municipalities were given statistics of the needs, we would have a regulated system. At the moment there are completely unregulated programs going on in little areas-none of which are going in any particular direction with any particular knowledge of what they are doing. In other words, I suggest that we are going simultaneously in a great many directions, spending a great deal of money and, consequently, not getting anywhere.
An example of the type of thing we have been doing is illustrated in Cornwall. I hope the hon. member for Stormont will correct me if I am wrong about this. They are there giving courses in barbering and meat-cutting to a limited number of people. In Brantford, 75 people are taking part in a retraining program in connection with radio and technical courses. I believe there are four courses. One course is for radio electronics and I believe another is for stenographic services.
They have no real knowledge of what they are doing. That is the trouble with this whole matter; there is confusion among the people who are to be retrained in these little municipal areas all over the country. These people will go out and find they cannot even get a job with the new skill they have acquired because this skill is already possessed by thousands of people who are on the labour market. Then there is also the question that automation has taken over in that particular job.
I think this problem has to be seriously considered. It has been said that education is a provincial matter. Yes, education is a provincial matter, but training is not education.

There is a difference between training and education. Training welders has very little to do with culture, very little to do with language and certainly nothing to do with religion. This is an area where a national program should be effected in terms of its organization. Who should be organizing it? Probably the mayor of the city. He, and people like him will be stuck with trying to work this training plan for the unemployed.
It may be an ad hoc solution, but is it a national solution? I do not think so. These people have not the time, and they have no idea what direction they should take. This is one field where you should have specialists, where people who have a real knowledge of the problem should move into the area and relate the needs of those to be trained to the needs of the nation as a whole and then set up a scheme adaptable to those requirements. Nothing of the sort envisaged by the present government is going to provide a solution of that kind. In any event, such a project will cost a great deal of money, and some are going to ask: is it worth it? May I read something written by Lord Beveridge which seems to me to be relevant?
To submit to unemployment or slums or want, to let children go hungry or the sick unattended for fear of increasing the internal national debt is to lose all sense of values.
I certainly agree with that comment. What are the solutions? Perhaps, I might also read the following:
-The state is obliged in as great a measure as possible to provide employment through public works which are useful to the community, and to facilitate, through advice and in other ways, the hiring of those who seek work.
That was a quotation from Pope Pius XII. What is the cost of unemployment? We shall be paying this cost, not so much now as in five or ten years from now. A Catholic service bureau in the Peterborough constituency accomplished a considerable piece of work when it undertook a survey of so-called "down and out" people. The bureau discovered that the great majority of these people had lost their jobs at the age of 35, or 40, and had never really got back into society. Instead they had become a burden to the community and dependent upon the social services provided.
What about the cost to business? We know that the rate of business failures has reached a level not known in the last 20 years. The rate of failure was 18 per cent higher than in January of last year. Doctors find their bills are not paid; teachers find their classes are crowded with people who have no hope of getting jobs and who are cluttering up the education system.

We are still mesmerized by the idea of a welfare state. It is ironic, but we still think that welfare is the answer and we are rushing to try to establish a welfare state at a time when the welfare state is to a large extent outmoded and ineffective in the twentieth century. I am not suggesting that payments now being made should be discontinued, but we have to plan so as to reach a stage where such payments will not be necessary. Let us take the present trends to a final conclusion; we shall find one quarter of the population working and paying unemployment insurance and three quarters of the population collecting it, on the basis of all that is being said about the changing labour markets today. This is the picture, and it is no use talking about socialism and free enterprise, because neither of those words has any reference to realities in Canada today.
We are still mouthing words which have absolutely no connotation.
When the Leader of the Opposition says we can work only in a free enterprise economic structure, that means nothing. We have not got a free enterprise system. No one wants socialism, either. What we do want is an intelligently planned economy which would make proper provision for the needs of our citizens.
I am surprised that so many references have been made recently to President Kennedy. I am surprised at all this enthusiasm for leftwing thinking. The Conservatives here usually regard themselves as being to the political right, but in the United States Mr. Kennedy is now being accused of being in the hands of labour. He is criticized as being too greatly under the influence of whitecollar socialists from Harvard. That is the sort of thing they are saying about Kennedy now.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-18, to provide for a Canadian lottery.
He said:
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill to the house, I cannot help remembering the many remarks made to me since I first mentioned my intention to have lotteries made legal in Canada.
Like my colleagues, I appreciate that, according to the letter and spirit of the Criminal Code we now have in Canada, it is illegal to organize, promote or allow lotteries. It is not my intention to recommend any infringement of the law. On the contrary, it is by submission to the law that we can best serve our political and parliamentary institutions. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is precisely because I am a staunch upholder of the law that I am moving this bill to have certain lotteries legalized.
This project first came to my mind when I was given a brief by the Joliette local of the national syndicates in 1958, recommending the establishment of a national lottery.

Private Bills
I have also read in the press that the international brotherhoods of railway employees have recommended a government lottery. The purpose of this bill is to provide for the establishment and operation of a Canadian lottery and sweepstakes. The bill provides that the governor in council shall appoint ten members of parliament to serve without pay as a commission; the commission would use the staff, property and facilities of the Canadian government and crown corporations to carry out its operations. After allowance for prizes, profits are apportioned among family allowance recipients and so on.
And then you could add to this bill-this is a matter of detail in case a lottery should become legal in Canada and a national lottery was established-that tickets could be sold through post offices, "caisses populaires" or banks.
As you all know, some time ago a large daily newspaper in Quebec, that is La Presse, investigated the matter and found that 98,780 people were in favour of a provincial lottery and 149 were against it. That was an unprecedented success.
I am sure that if La Presse had carried out such an investigation to find out whether the public was in favour of a national lottery, their success would also have been an unprecedented one.
La Presse certainly deserves to be congratulated for calling the public's attention to the matter, while making it possible to debate the matter and find out how it rates with public opinion.
I shall not go over all the arguments that were brought forth again and again in favour of or against a national lottery. I am fully aware that you know them as well as I do. I only want to point out that at one time lotteries were allowed in Canada and that the people who bought tickets then were not any more venturesome or reckless than the people today. There were quite a few lotteries, such as the people's lottery, the province of Quebec lottery, the popular lottery, the Mount Royal lottery, and all those lotteries paid thousands of dollars to the lucky winners, while the promoters collected thousands of dollars, generally used for charitable purposes.
I am not suggesting that the authorities of the time were wanting in foresight when they decided to prohibit lotteries in this

country; nor am I suggesting that they were prompted by petty interests that had nothing to do with the lotteries themselves; I shall merely point out that the situation has changed since then.
Today, lotteries are illegal. And what happens? Tell me frankly. Is there any member in this house who has not been offered at some time or other lottery tickets from other countries? I shall not ask those who have bought tickets to rise, but you know as well as I do that this country is full of agents for foreign lotteries who sell millions of dollars worth of tickets annually and who drain our money out of the country. And yet hardly a month goes by without the papers reporting that Mr. So-and-so, perhaps the brother's father or Miss So-and-so won the grand prize in the Irish sweepstakes or the Navy lottery. In every case it is our dollars that are going out of the country. In our estimation about $90 million in Canadian money go to foreign countries every year. In my opinion, we must put a stop to that bleeding of the Canadian people's money to the profit of other countries.
Our people are neither more evil nor more timid than others, and they are as fascinated by games of chance as the people of France, the United States or South America.
Our people like to risk a few cents, even a few dollars, and that is so much money going out of Canada.
Don't you worry, our laws will never prevent our people from betting. They will bet on horses, boxers, hockey games and baseball games. There are even some who bet on federal elections.
The bill I have the honour to introduce in the house is not designed to encourage vice or make people spend. Such an idea is very far from my mind. This bill is based to some extent on the desire of our people, as elsewhere in the world, to bet on things that are particularly unpredictable, but where the element of chance can be reduced through serious study.
Between you and me, a bet is always a bet, and those who indulge in that game must be prepared to lose as well as to win.
Lotteries are the expression of that instinct people have of taking a chance, and often the risk is very slim in proportion to what it may yield.

Private Bills
In allowing the organization of national lotteries in Canada, for certain charitable or social purposes, or as mentioned in this bill to increase family allowances, the Canadian parliament would, at the same time, keep in Canada those thousands of dollars now going abroad, which would represent an important factor in our economy.
However, there is one thing we should not overlook. In order to be successful and efficient, a real lottery should cover the whole country. In fact, if the federal parliament decided to pass legislation to allow the provinces to organize lotteries within their territory, we would then be faced with a terrible problem of displacement of funds.
Just imagine for a moment that Quebec and Ontario should organize lotteries, in order to help hospitals or for other charitable purposes, while other provinces would not. What would happen? You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, that people of those provinces having no lotteries would hasten to buy tickets in provinces where lotteries exist and you would then have, within the country, important movements of funds, which might jeopardize the financial position of provinces having no lotteries. Such a situation would hardly be desirable.
However, this does not mean I am opposed to provincial lotteries.
Therefore, I believe that if the bill I have the honour to introduce is adopted-and I do hope it will be, naturally-I think the federal parliament will have to arrange for a huge national lottery to be held in order that all Canadians, from coast to coast, may have the opportunity of taking part in it. With one stone, we could kill two birds. We could help finance the charitable organizations selected, or attain such other purpose as may have been designated. Participating Canadians might have a chance to get the lucky ticket.
Here are, in a few words, Mr. Speaker, some of the reasons which prompted me to submit this bill. I wish we could all study it in the same spirit and with the same open mind.
I would also be grateful to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Bell) if he would, in the course of this debate, let us know what he thinks of this bill and the establishment of national lotteries in Canada.
