speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the two hon. members who have placed
90205-6-1834
on the order paper resolutions to allow lotteries in Canada. I refer to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) whose bill is now before the house, and the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie), who is unfortunately kept home by sickness.
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to what the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm had to say. One can disagree with the views expressed by the hon. member in connection with the bill introduced today, but that is not the point. At this stage of the second reading of the bill, it is the principle of the legislation that should be discussed. And it is in that light that I want to talk briefly about the present bill.
The assertion of the hon. member that wagering and betting are here to stay cannot be denied. According to the hon. member, bets are taken even on federal election results. I would add that it is also the case with provincial election results. Perhaps the hon. member could have said more about this.
Mr. Speaker, like many other members of this house who are interested in this matter I am thinking of all the things that are needed in Canada, particularly in the provinces, and of the steps that could be taken to bring about new sources of revenues. Speaking of lotteries, one can admit nowadays that no genuine principle stands in the way of a lottery. I will even go a little further. Reference is made to an amendment to section 179 of the Criminal Code. That section to all practical purposes is inoperative at this time. Why then should we delude ourselves? Why not face the problem?
If I remember correctly, one of our learned professors of political economy, Mr. Edouard Montpetit, told us one day during a lesson on public economy: "The best law in the world becomes inoperative if it is not based on the psychology of the masses". It is quite clear that today-and we should be fair enough to admit it-we ourselves take a hand in foreign sweepstakes, whether they be Irish or English, in defiance of section 197 of the Criminal Code.
In these circumstances, I think we must be realistic and consider that question on the basis of our needs.
My hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm mentioned the poll initiated recently by the newspaper La Presse in the province of Quebec. It is quite revealing that close to 100,000 people who gave their name and address, expressed their wish to see a lottery organized in Quebec. That brings up a very important consideration. I see many problems at this time in the establishment

Private Bills
of a federal lottery. We must have regard for the views expressed by some provinces which do not seem prepared to agree. Well, in Quebec, we are ready and I do not see why an amendment to the Criminal Code could not be introduced permitting the establishment of a lottery in order to give effect to the wish expressed by the people of the province of Quebec.
In answer to a question I addressed him recently, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) replied that as a matter of fact, he had exchanged unofficial communications with some premiers on the matter of a lottery. On the other hand, the premier of Quebec stated himself recently that he had talked the question over with the Minister of Justice.
If Quebec taxpayers are in favour of this idea, if the legislature of the province of Quebec is in favour of a lottery, I trust that the premier of Quebec will make a formal request for it to the federal government.
During the discussion on the Canadian bill of rights, several hon. members would have liked to have a national bill of rights, and we recall that the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) then said: "For our part, we are ready. There are certain provinces which apparently are not ready yet. So, we will take the lead."
And, to go one better, at the recent federal-provincial conference the Prime Minister said to the premiers: "You will now have the task of finding your income sources in your respective provinces."
Consequently, this is a way to enable the people of Quebec to get organized, a way to meet their wishes and their needs.
Since we have to decide at this stage on the principle of lotteries, I trust that all hon. members will wish to make known the assent of this house. This is a popular question in Canada today.
May I point out to my hon. friends that many newspapers report the reactions of many Canadians to the effect that there is nothing more deplorable than certain bills submitted to this house being talked out without any decision being arrived at.
On this question of lottery, why should we not take our responsibilities, why should we not adopt today the principle of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm?
I do not wish to unduly lengthen this speech but in conclusion, I simply want to read a few lines from an item that appeared in La Presse of February 15, following a public poll held in the province of Quebec. The article reads as follows:
Quebec is in favour of a lottery and that is something that the people's representatives, whether they sit on municipal councils, in the provincial legislature or in the House of Commons, must or should realize. Since that poll enabled the taxpayers to enlighten their representatives, they in turn, are bound to inform their governments and bring the necessary pressure to bear upon them.
Is there any need to spell it out? That question is beyond all party politics.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks, I wish to say that, to a certain extent, the members are bound by the wish or will of the taxpayers when it is clearly indicated.
Well, those of us particularly who are from Quebec, have received a very clear mandate to try to obtain, through our pressures and requests, that section 179 of the Criminal Code be amended, in order to allow the establishment of a lottery. That is what we are doing today, that is what I, for one, am doing, and what I intend to do whenever the opportunity arises. And I hope, as I said a moment ago, that before long the province of Quebec, through the action of its legislature, will submit to the government of Canada an official request indicating the wish and will of the province of Quebec to establish a lottery in that province.

speechtext:
About 230 years ago an English writer, Henry Fielding, turned out a verse that expressed some opinion on lotteries and it might be well to lead off by reading that verse:
A lottery is a taxation Upon all the fools in creation;
And heaven be praised It is easily raised.
Credulity's always in fashion For folly's a fund,
Will never lose ground,
While fools are so rife in the nation.
This is a most interesting bill that the hon. member has introduced. I think perhaps the most intriguing part of it is that it would tend to encourage something which we had on a much larger scale in Toronto in the thirties when everyone there was much exercised about the baby derby. There were prizes put up by a well known Torontonian which led to a test amongst the mothers to see who could have the most children in so many years. This was a rather outrageous situation

but it led to giving the popular press a great deal of scope for publicity and we certainly learned a lot about the problems of mothers who have children on such a regular basis.
The purpose of this bill would really be to provide funds for those parents who had large families-

maintopic: LOTTERY

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: LOTTERY
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN LOTTERY COMMISSION
speechtext:
I am going to give the subject fairly complete coverage and I will tell the hon. member where I stand. It seems to me that the purpose to which the lottery would be dedicated is such a highly specialized one that I feel I could be much more sympathetic to the bill the hon. member introduced last year. As he will remember, that bill was linked more directly with charitable purposes. In so far as lotteries are concerned, it seems to me any lottery is a form of gambling. The participants pay money for the privilege of trying for prizes which are given on the basis of chance. There is no skill or cleverness required. Such sweepstakes are based completely on chance.
A prime example of this practice right across the country is the game of bingo. There are all kinds of games going on at the present time that are very much like this game of chance. I think everybody in the House of Commons knows that one is continually being solicited to buy tickets for hockey pools, football pools, the Irish sweepstakes and the very well known Quebec sweepstakes. The point of my remarks is that gambling seems to be inherent in the human nature. There was an article in the Montreal press the other day based upon the theory that the four men who had been murdered in recent weeks were tied up with the numbers game racket. I believe that is some form of lottery.
Surely there is not an hon. member who has not some organization in his home town that is dunning him to buy a ticket for something like an afghan, a bond or a car. The prevalence of these things in the world today is tremendous. If, as Fielding said, lottery is a taxation upon all the fools in creation, then Canada is loaded with fools. The whole question seems to be involved in the approach the hon. member is taking and I think, myself, that in so far as the problem of football pools is concerned-which seems to be involved in the negotiations between Mr. Lesage and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton)-we should put this on some kind of legal basis and get the most out of it.
Private Bills
The question as to whether it should be put on a legal basis is the real crux of the matter. We can look to examples in other democracies that have a longer tradition than our own. At the present time in Great Britain the equivalent of the Minister of Finance has his own field of lottery because if you buy government bonds you are entitled to participate in a draw and if the serial number of your bond is drawn you may earn a substantial sum of money as well as invest in the nation. Ever since 1934 Sweden has had a semi-official lottery and the proceeds are used to support certain charitable institutions. In Britain itself there are the football pools which are an example of a lottery. Some of us think there is an element or a modicum of skill in it, although I think it is capable of exaggeration. When I was in England for several years I enjoyed playing the football pools. I looked forward to the regular custom early in the week of filling out my chart. I do not feel it harmed me or any of the millions of the people in Britain who take part in these particular football pools.
The main reason for the banning of the old lotteries, especially in England in 1823, was the triumph of puritan middle class morality. The other factor that was involved was that legalized forms of gambling of another kind connected with dog racing or horse racing came into effect and the jockey clubs have always been the bitter enemies of the lotteries because they siphoned off a great deal of their take. I have always been amused by the fact that horsemen improving the breed for racing purposes must depend so much upon the gambling revenue that comes in from the tote machines, the pari-mutuel or whatever the system may be. There is nothing wrong with this, and it has been established as a legal form of gambling in Canada for many years. What is the difference between gambling on a horse and buying a ticket on a lottery? Apparently it is the modicum of skill that is involved. I have not met so many successful horseplayers who were satisfied with their skill that one could be really sure on this point. This seems to be the only distinguishing mark we can make between buying a lottery ticket and taking a flyer on a horse.
Here again the British are much more liberal and open about this. It is possible to get in touch with a bookie very easily at the racetrack, the corner store or at some official betting agency. Again, I do not believe Britain has had any great moral breakdown or corruption as a result of this form of gambling, that is what you might call the skilled kind of gambling. This would suggest

Private Bills
to me that those who feel that the legalization of lotteries would lead to a break-down in morality are all wrong.
I do not feel that the reasons for the strong opposition to lotteries by the Protestant sects are so related to theological subjects as they are to certain moral rules. Superficially, it might appear strange that religious groups stressing the freedom of the individual to choose his own means of finding God and insisting on the individual's right to worship in his own way should be their brother's keeper in the field of morals. A similar attitude was once noticeable toward insurance, card playing, dancing and still exists toward the drinking of alcoholic beverages. We still have within the protestant sects moral rules that condemn these practices.
I think all who have looked at it historically are aware of the fact this is part of the puritan tradition which is over four centuries old and which still has a great deal of vitality in this country. I think Homan Catholicism tends to take a less jaundiced view of drinking and gambling, perhaps assuming from its long history that these are minor vices.
The Catholic and Protestant attitudes are pertinent to any assessment of the chances for legal lotteries in Canada because strongest support for them comes from Catholic Quebec, strongest opposition from the organized Protestant clergy in the rest of Canada and from newspaper editors who follow their lead. If hon. members want illustrations of this fact, they could go to the various reports of committees which were held and which went into this subject fairly thoroughly. They will find that most of the strongest opposition to lotteries came from mostly ministerial spokesmen for the Protestant groups.
Clergymen and newspaper editors are very influential in swaying legislatures. However, it is also a fact that the moral code of today is less stern than it was 30 years, 40 years or 50 years ago. I think many of us who have followed the newspapers would agree that the newspaper editors have not led the way in relaxing the morals code. In the advertising pages I think there has been a move towards relaxation but not in the editorial pages. I think the same thing holds good in so far as the protestant clergy are concerned.
In recent decades the province of Quebec has taken a great interest in lotteries and several times the provincial government there has tried to have passed bills that would make them legal. The Criminal Code is drawn up by parliament in Ottawa. However, it is put in practice through provincial attorneys general. I think this is one reason

why, if you get a province that takes a lenient view of lotteries or raffles, it is unlikely that you will ever get any lottery promoters prosecuted. I think this is why in Quebec you have so many lotteries or raffles. I know that the few times I have been in Montreal during the hockey season there seemed to be a bewildering variety of lotteries or hockey pools in operation. I think the same situation applies in almost all big cities.
The last time that lotteries were a big political issue in Ottawa was back in 1934 when the Senate sent to the House of Commons a bill that would have let provincial authorities set their own course with any lotteries designed for aiding hospitals. I have here copies of that bill and I actually intended to introduce the same bill this year until I discovered that my intention had been, let us say, preceded by the intention of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) and by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne). In 1934 Mr. Bennett was prime minister and Mr. Mackenzie King was leader of the opposition. They let it be known that the whole matter was going to be decided on a free vote. The measure was defeated, 105 votes to 57 votes, with almost all the support coming from Quebec members. The vote might have been closer if Mr. Bennett and Mr. King each, as private members, had not spoken against it. Mr. Bennett stressed that his decision was based not on "absolute right or wrong", but on the fact that lotteries had a sorry history, as indeed they have back in the 19th century even in Britain and in Italy. Mr. King was concerned, as one might imagine he would be, knowing the delicate nature of his sensitivities, with the unsettling nature of lotteries. He said:
What we require in the affairs of individuals and of the nation is less of uncertainty and more of certainty ... less of reliance on chance and luck, and more reliance on judgment and effort.
That is in context the Protestant ministerial moral line on the whole matter of lotteries. Mr. King went on to state a theme that ran throughout the entire debate of the subject:
There is no doubt that much of the distress of the times has come about through excessive speculation . .. for too many people . . . have got into the habit or relying upon chance and gambling in one form or another.
The Canadian parliament, influenced by the great crash of 1929 and the subsequent depression, identified the basis of sweepstakes with stock-market speculation. As Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, leader of the C.C.F., put it, if one decried the one, one had to decry the other; that is, if one was against playing the stock market, one pretty well had to be against the idea of the lottery.

Actually, the vital difference between a sweepstake and a stock market speculation is that the latter, like bridge-playing, chess, or even betting on the horses, allows some room for skill or inside knowledge. For some reason, this tends to give such forms of gambling a superior prestige over the forms that are based on pure chance. Depending on the prosperity of your society at the time, there is greater or smaller concern over the fact that no matter how skilful the speculation, it is true in most cases that someone has to lose. One should remember that at one time the insurance business had to be conducted secretly because it was considered to involve forbidden wagers against the outcome of events. Even joint stock companies were once held by religious authorities to be immoral organizations just as, I am sure all members of the house know, at one time Christianity condemned usury or the taking of interest.
In any discussion of the fundamentals of gambling one must come to grips with a mystery called nature. Nature, or the unpredictability of such things as weather and man's behaviour, has always made much of each person's life a gamble, or better, left it open to chance or luck. This is an element with which we are all extremely familiar. It is the common denominator of the whole human experience. I refer to this question of luck or chance. I think it is instinctive with us as human beings that we are willing to take a chance. I suppose the greatest gamble of all is what Haskell used; that is the greatest gamble was related to the belief that God existed. But whatever the case may be, we as human beings are always prepared to take these risks. Yet because of Puritan and moral concepts, we have hesitated to legalize these things and to set up any framework through which we can take decent advantage of them.
I would put it to members of this house that Fielding's remarks about lotteries being a taxation upon all the fools in creation may have some validity; but what sort of tax upon our foolishness is the situation in which four men are murdered in one of our modern cities because they are mixed up with something that is conducted below the level of the eyes of the law? It seems to me that we have strong grounds today, in judging human nature and the Canadian situation, for saying that it is time that we had lotteries and that we used the revenue from them for good and sound purposes. I can think of a number of sound purposes that are obvious; for instance in connection with hospitals, medical research and sports as the British and Swedes do with their football pools, with their general amateur athletic enterprises.

In other words there are any number of good things that we could choose for our lotteries and I think such lotteries would strike the common denominator and interest of all Canadians.
Since 1946, the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion has held polls of public opinion on the question of government lotteries. In the first poll there was a majority of only 52 per cent but in the recent ones the appeal has become stronger and stronger. I have just forgotten the exact figures with regard to the last one, but it now appears that almost two thirds of Canadians whose opinions have been sampled by this particular organization would be in favour of some kind of lottery. One of the things that frightens me-

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member whether he is talking about lotteries with some public objective or just lotteries in general?

speechtext:
I am talking about lotteries with a public objective; that is to say lotteries sponsored by the government. One of the problems in connection with legalizing lotteries is this. We might have the prospect of a whole host of various provincial lotteries.
This could create a great deal of difficulty. It would create difficulty, for example, if we had enabling legislation, through the Criminal Code, allowing provincial attorneys general to support this measure. We could have, say, a massive lottery for hospitals in Quebec. In order to reach out and give the lottery the widest possible financial basis they would be selling tickets right across the nation, one would hope and perhaps one would expect, and yet we would be faced with a problem something like that of the question of coloured or non-coloured margarine because these tickets would be going into other jurisdictions.
For that reason I feel strongly that if we are going to have a government lottery it would have to be somewhat along the line set out in the hon. member's bill; that is, something on a national rather than a provincial scale. But we would hope that the benefits of the lottery would go to institutions that might fall within the provincial framework.
Of course, one of the most important questions in relation to legalizing lotteries is this. What will legalized lotteries do to the illegal lotteries which support so many charitable and group association endeavours at the present time? It seems to me that this is something about which we know very little. An inquiry would almost of necessity have to be undertaken in this connection before we supported a measure such as this on

Private Bills
third reading. It we did have a large scale legal lottery in Canada, where tickets were sold across the breadth of the nation, what would this do to the church bingos, the ladies' raffles and even the political parties raffles? I know that all three political parties in our part ot the country have at various times conducted, or are conducting raffles or lotteries of a sort. This question, of course, is something that I cannot assess.
However, I do not think a well established national lottery based upon something such as the Grey Cup or the Queen's Plate classic in the spring, or events such as these would necessarily interfere with local lotteries that are carried on at the present time and which in many places are the lifeblood of service clubs and associations.
I know that in our city every spring there is a contest sponsored by a reputable service club in which one has to guess when the first ship is going to arrive in the harbour. I understand that in one of the western provinces there is a very large lottery in connection with when the break-up is going to hit a certain place on the river. We do have these lotteries. My own feeling is that a national lottery based on three or four events would not cripple the lotteries held by other organizations.
In conclusion I should like to mention something about the British premium savings bonds. This is a form of government lottery. One of the odd things is that the Canadian government allows these British bonds to be sold in Canada. They can be purchased through a Canadian bank for dollars and any prize money will be paid in dollars. I understand the top prize is $14,000.
In other words, here in Canada you can play the British treasury's bond game. That is another example of a breach that has been made in this question of lotteries being illegal. It seems to me that we have here another instance of a situation where we are ready for legislation that recognizes the interest of the Canadian people on this whole question of lotteries.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for sponsoring the bill. There is one part of the bill about which I and some of my colleagues are in a little doubt. That is the matter of whether the reward or surplus from the lotteries should be apportioned among family allowance recipients according to a scale that increases with the number of children in the family who are qualified to receive allowances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with this bill I should first like to say that I do not see any difference between lotteries and many other activities that are carried on today in our country. In this connection I share the same opinion as service clubs and many other people throughout the country.
Everyone is free to dispose of his money as he sees fit. It has been argued that life itself is a gamble. Whether you invest your money in trade, on the stock exchange or any other avenue of activity, you certainly take a chance. I do not think there is anything wrong in the principle of spending a little money on a lottery, say to the amount of one or two dollars a year. I will go further and say that in years of expensive living such as we are going through, there is something to be said in favour of allowing a person to introduce into his life the element of hope and ambition that comes to him from spending a little money on a lottery.
I remember buying a ticket on a car lottery. I paid $1 for the ticket and from the time I bought it to the time the car was raffled I dreamt all day that I was going to win that car. I received a great deal of enjoyment out of the dollar I spent on that ticket. I do not think it did me any harm, and I am sure that, like myself, many people received enjoyment although they did not win the car either.
We often read and hear about the Irish sweepstake results. I am very happy that many of the people who win are not in the rich class. As a result of being fortunate enough to win the sweepstake they are able to enjoy a happy time for the rest of their days. We also read that older people have been able to enjoy happiness for the rest of their lives through winning a sweepstake.
I feel that a lottery under government control, where a great share of the profits would go to the establishment of hospitals, their building and maintenance, to those people who are in need of welfare, to building homes for the aged, or to some other useful public

service, would be of great public benefit. The fact that the law governing lotteries is not being obeyed by the public proves that it is not a popular law. You cannot enforce a law that is against popular opinion.
You can trade on the stock exchange, you can bet on the horse races, or you can take part in the games of chance at fairs. You can do these things as much as you like and there seems to be no harm in them; there is no danger of demoralizing our young people. But when you buy one or two tickets on a lottery conducted by a public organization, it is said that our young people are being poisoned morally and socially.
I mentioned betting on the horse races. My hon. friend mentioned this and he said it was a matter of skill. I have been to the horse races and I have placed a $2 bet on the horses. I have seen other people bet $2 on the horses. Well, I did not collect very often. Sometimes you receive $4, but most of the time you see people there who cannot afford to be betting. They are betting on these horses coming in, and they cannot really afford it.
I am not by any means against horse racing, but I would draw to the attention of hon. members that if we are going to have one form of gambling, why cannot we have another? I have mentioned the games of chance to be found at fairs. That matter is a disgrace to this country. I am certainly against this type of betting. You go through these fairs and come to the barkers at the side-shows. You cannot get away from them. You take your family to the fair and go to the sideshow and you hear the barker say, "Come on over and win. I will give you a free chance." You see there people who cannot afford to spend their money in this way. They walk over to the barker at the sideshow and he says, "Here you are; now pick up a clothes pin". The fellow reaches over and picks up a clothes pin. The barker gets all excited and says, "Yes, you are fortunate You have just won $25. It has not cost you anything. Now, if you give me $5 you can have another clothespin to take off, and you might get a hundred." He gets another off, and the man says: "that is wonderful; now if you go on you have a chance of winning a wonderful wristwatch". It can go on like this for hour after hour, and I have seen ladies crying when they left those stands because their husbands had spent every penny in their pockets. We can allow this kind of thing yet we cannot allow people to spend a dollar on a sweeepstake ticket. What harm would there be in allowing the sale of sweepstake tickets at a dollar? You might win $140,000 and get some enjoyment out of it.

By legalizing lotteries in Canada we would first of all ensure large sums being made available for the maintenance of our hospitals and educational institutions, funds from a source which today contributes absolutely nothing to these purposes. In the second place, such a law would allow people to do legally what they are today doing illegally.
I am referring, of course, to small pools on the results of hockey games, bingos and the like. In the third place, such legalisation would, to a large extent, stop the spending of Canadian money on tickets for lotteries run by other countries.
A lottery run under government supervision would mean honest and absolute control. It would attract to Canada millions of foreign dollars. It would supplement the dollars now being contributed by the taxpayer and bring millions into federal and provincial treasuries. In 1931 about $20 million was awarded in prize money in the Irish sweepstakes. More than $7,300,000 went to hospitals from the sale of tickets. We have hospitals and homes for the aged in this country. I read in the paper the other day that the city of Calgary has no more room for the sick in its hospitals and that cases have to be sent to Edmonton. We need hospitals, and how better could we raise the money than through sweepstakes restricted to once or twice a year, as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) suggested.
A royal commission formed to inquire into the sale of Irish sweepstake tickets in the United Kingdom found that the total sales in connection with the first eight sweepstakes amounted to approximately $90 million. That will illustrate how much money goes from one country to another when events of this kind are involved. If we permitted sweepstakes to be made legal in our country we would see this money coming into our treasuries to provide help for hospitals and other much needed projects.
No one can convince me that the spending of from $1 to $5 a year on lottery tickets by any citizen of this country will tend to demoralize him, his family or his neighbours. I wonder if the people who oppose lotteries have ever been shocked by the hopeless outlook of those of our fellow citizens who have lost their last nickel and mortgaged their future by gambling on the stock exchange, the grain exchange, the mining exchange and similar institutions. The hon. member for Port Arthur suggested that people were gambling on these things. Others say that a great deal of skill enters into it. That may be so, but after all there is skill attached to horse racing. However that may be, the percentage of people who gamble on these

exchanges when they clearly have not got the required skill must be very great.
